en: Preface to the *Deciding Record of the Profound Commentary on the Lotus Sūtra*, written by the monk Sangzhu of Longxing Monastery in Yangzhou. Regarding the term "deciding" (*jueze*):
it refers to supplementing the *Profound Commentary* (*Xuanzan*) in order to provide an exposition. Since the sūtra was transmitted to the Eastern Xia (China), its analysis has been quite extensive.

Extensive yet singularly overseeing the spirit-platform, far surpassing all other views—could this be anything other than the profound *Xuanzan*? In matters, one must follow antiquity; thus, the *Benlun* (Treatise on the Origin) serves as the guiding compass.
In teaching, there must be a basis for reliance; thus, the various scriptures serve as the standard. Its meaning is rich while its prose is concise;
its principles are deep while its diction is elegant. One looks up at it and rarely glimpses its boundaries; one draws from it and cannot fathom its surging waves. Thus it is seen.
That which is esteemed throughout the world and suspended like the sun and moon—how could it have come about without cause?

As for those who applied themselves with profound reflection and refined investigation, who fished in the deep and sought out the hidden, and who attained that which was not easily won—it was due to the Great Master of India. This Great Master dwelt in steadfast integrity through rigorous asceticism.

Displaying humility and nurturing rectitude, the Tripitaka Master of the Great Tang translated treatises and sutras whose meanings were neither partial nor complete, and whose sections were neither large nor small.

Whatever passed his ears was necessarily recited from his mouth; whatever met his eyes was necessarily understood by his mind. When he annotated them, his feelings were never overfilled; when he drew upon them, his wisdom was never exhausted.
In the leisure between widely propagating [the teachings], he sighed and said: "Now, the images of the *Yi* are empty and non-substantial; they still rely upon..."
The *Huantuan* (Commentary on the Hexagrams) states: "How much more so for this praise of the profound and abstruse; it does not rely upon the basket or the trap.

Accordingly, I have extensively examined ancient lore and selected new interpretations, appending them to this text and making decisions accordingly. This shall enable scholars who transmit the scriptures not to wait to gird their robes [at the master's feet], and allow disciples who carry their books upon their backs to be able to open up unique insights.
It is as bright and pure as the full moon in the autumn sky, and as clear and illuminating as a shining torch.

This lamp is for those within the dark chamber. The drafting of this preface is complete. It was proofread by the disciple Faqing. As for Master Jin: his understanding and practice, his virtue and conduct, place him as one who follows in the footsteps of the Master.
Day by day he has spoken of learning, yet he does not yet dare claim to surpass his former teachers (the "blue" dyeing the "indigo").

Through years of accumulating the merit of his understanding, he has ascended to a level nearly equal to that of the Sublime Sages. Having heard and propagated the Tripitaka for more than ten years, how could it be that only the Ten Disciples have spread their own renown?
Regarding Confucius, his four disciples were merely praised by Kumārajīva; yet whenever there was a pause in his formal exegesis, he would discourse on profound metaphysical principles (*xuanli*).

Although he had received these teachings orally from the former masters, they were lost to the brush and not recorded in writing. I, being fortunate enough to attend at the edge of the courtyard, have with earnest sincerity requested [these records].
It was then expanded into eight fascicles, forming a complete body of work. This was initiated and discussed by the Great Master from India;
it was refined and embellished by the Vinaya master Master Qing. Through these two worthies, the meaning was rendered exhaustive.
This was during the first month of spring in the third year of the Dali era of our Tang Dynasty’s reign over heaven.
Commentary on the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka-sūtra*: A Record of Decisive Selection, Scroll One.
Compiled by the Śramaṇa Chongjun of Tiantzhu Monastery in Hangzhou;
with annotations collected by the Śramaṇa Faching of Chanzhi Monastery in Yangzhou.

First, let us explain this preface. The first two characters serve as the opening of the discourse. From "To realize the provisional and the true" (*jue quan zhen*) downward, the actual subject matter is presented.

Regarding the phrase "I have heard" (*gai wen*): generally, in the composition of texts, expressions such as "I have heard," "privately considering," and so forth, are all terms used to show that one does not exalt oneself.
Thus, in the *Commentary on the Classic of Filial Piety*, it says: "The filial piety of the Son of Heaven is characterized by humility. Alternatively, "gai" (perhaps) may be used as a contraction.
Thus, the *Xuanjing* (Mysterious Classic) and the *Xiaojing* (Classic of Filial Piety) state: “Gai” means “brevity.

This implies that while the filial duties of a Son of Heaven as expounded by the Son of Heaven are immeasurable, what is being discussed here is merely presented in brief. Furthermore, the phrase “I have heard” (*gao wen*) is also taken in its sense of brevity;
for although the Buddhist teachings are indeed vast and manifold, they are now explained in summary. Therefore, it says “below,” and so forth. [End of] Chen.

Within this exposition, there are two general divisions. First, up to the words "Is it not so? (*zhě hū*), there is a general summary of the intent of the teaching. Second, from the words "First, as for the title" (*shǒu chēng xià*) onwards, there is the formal explanation of the title.
Within the first division, there are again two parts. The first consists of four phrases, which clarify the manifestation of the body and the establishment of the teaching.

The second, from the words "Shaking open the mountains" (*zhèn róng shān xià*) onwards, extensively reveals the essential meaning of the sūtra. Within the first part, the initial two phrases concern the manifestation of the body, while the latter two phrases concern the establishment of the teaching.

Regarding the phrase "the commentary reaches the manifestation of the Awakened One": this refers to the appearance of his physical form. "The Awakened One" (*zhìjué*) refers to ultimate awakening. Now, there are three types of awakening;

because the Tathāgata’s awakening and practice are perfected to the utmost, he differs from ordinary beings, those of the two vehicles, and bodhisattvas, and is therefore called the "Ultimate Awakened One.

As for "expedient means" (*quán*): originally this did not exist, but it is manifested in response to sentient beings, and is thus called "expedient. As for "truth" (*zhēn*): it is the realization of reality.
Collectively, these are termed "True. One interpretation states that "Ultimate Enlightenment" (*zhìjué*) is the general designation for the three bodies (*trikāya*).

How is this known? In Sanskrit, *buddha* means "enlightened" (*jué*). This is because all three bodies are indeed Buddha. The provisional refers to the *nirmāṇakāya* (transformation body), while the true refers to the *saṃbhogakāya* (reward body).

However, having accumulated causes over three *asaṃkhyeya-kalpas* until merit was perfected and the Way fulfilled, it is in contrast to the *nirmāṇabuddha* (transformation Buddha) that [the True Body] is thus obtained.

Regarding the "True Name" (Zhēnmíng): Question: Why are only the Transformation Body (*nirmāṇakāya*) and the Reward Body (*saṃbhogakāya*) mentioned, while the Dharma Buddha (*dharmakāya*) is not explained?

Answer: The Dharma Body is the root, while the Reward and Transformation Bodies are the branches. The root is the essential nature (*tattva*), which is profoundly still and cannot be discussed in terms of being accomplished or unaccomplished.

Now, because we wish to respond to sentient beings through speech, we speak only of the Transformation and Reward Bodies; thus, this is based on the branches to provide clarification, rather than discussing the root.

Each [explanation] relies on a specific meaning, yet they do not contradict one another. Some say that "ultimate awakening" is the same as before; regarding the "provisional and real," these possess the three bodies (*trikāya*).

That is to say, the transformation body (*nirmāṇakāya*) and the enjoyment body for others (*parasaṃbhogakāya*) are both termed "provisional," while the enjoyment body for oneself (*svasaṃbhogakāya*) and the dharma body (*dharmakāya*) are both termed "real.

Question: For what reason is this so? Answer: Because the Buddha in his enjoyment body for others and the transformation body act as responses for those at the ten stages (*daśabhūmi*) and for the followers of the two vehicles (*dviyāna*).

It is appropriate. Therefore, they are collectively termed "expedient" (*upāya*). As for the Buddha of self-enjoyment and the Dharma-body Buddha: having fulfilled the fruit as a recompense for the cause, they enjoy the bliss of the Dharma for themselves;
abiding eternally at the limit of reality (*bhūtakoṭi*), they are forever severed from faults and transgressions.

Thus, these two bodies are collectively named "real. Consequently, within these two terms—expedient and real—the three bodies are fully contained. Furthermore, it is said: "Ultimate awakening is the reward body (*saṃbhogakāya*); the expedient is the transformation body (*nirmāṇakāya*); the real is [the Dharma-body]."

The Dharma-body. Now, since the fruit of Buddhahood is not achieved spontaneously but must be attained through the cultivation of causes, even though Great Compassion is already perfected, it must logically respond to sentient beings.
When this response benefits others, the merit is traced back to its source, which lies in the Dharma-body.
Thus, the intended meaning of the sequential order of the three bodies is found herein. Each of the three explanations provided above possesses its own specific purport.
If one follows the intended meaning of the treatise, the first two explanations are superior; yet if one seeks it through the underlying principle, the latter interpretation is also acceptable.

For now, I have briefly discussed the intent of the treatise to enlighten those who are still ignorant. The extensive meanings therein shall be analyzed below. The same applies to all other cases; students should understand this.
"Bian" (辨) means to rely upon. "Ji" (機) refers to the faculty or root. "Dangsheng" (誕生) means birth. According to the *Yupian*, it also means faith. Furthermore, it signifies traces or footprints.
Now, the essence of Perfect Enlightenment contains both the provisional and the real. When intending to deliver sentient beings, it must rely upon their faculties to manifest for their benefit.
Since the conditions of their roots have matured, he manifested his birth in the royal palace; thus it is said.

The commentary on the *Lingshu* (The Mysterious Pivot), from "Mastering the Subtlety" to "Raising the Fish-Snare," concerns the establishment of the teaching. "Ling" (Mysterious) refers to its spiritual wonder; "Shu" (Pivot) refers to its pivotal mechanism.

This is the pivot of eloquence taught by the Tathāgata, comparable to the bright aperture through which a door-panel turns in the world today—just as a door can both open and close, so too does the Buddha's teaching function.
Because it can manifest according to circumstances, it is called a "pivotal mechanism. Thus, the *Book of Changes* (*Zhouyi*) says: "The pivotal mechanism..."
The source of honor and disgrace. It is further said: "Horizontally it is called the opening; vertically it is called the bolt. A bolt is the pivot. As the Book says:
"A foot-long pivot can control two doors; an inch-long axle-pin can support a pair of wheels. "Shan" (擅) means exclusive or solitary.

Because the Buddha is exclusively wondrous, he is like the term "exclusive city" (*zhuan-cheng*) applied to those who rule alone. Because the Buddha is uniquely wondrous, it is also like the case of a duel... [text ends]

The rooster wins because it takes precedence in crowing; thus, as in the expressions "to take sole responsibility for this matter" or "to do this alone," it should be called *qièyìng* (correspondence).
*Qún* means many. *Pǐn* refers to categories of things. *Yáng* means to raise up. *Quán* is the tool used for catching fish.

*Quán* (筌) refers to fragrant grass; *líng* (鈴) refers to the crossbar (*héng*) of a carriage. This is established in the *Yuán Yù Piān* (Explaining Jade Dictionary). Here, we take the character with the "bamboo" radical (*zhú*); the others are not used here.

Below, within the broad exposition of the essential meaning of the scripture, there are two parts: first, a specific narration of the scripture’s intent; second, from the phrase "from the *zǎo* and *shàn*" (*藻掞*) downward, a general exposition.
Victory. In the first [section], there are five parts. First, six lines concern the parable of the medicinal herbs; second, two lines concern the parable of the conjured city;
third, two lines concern the parable of the burning house; fourth, one line concerns the parable of the jewel in the topknot; fifth, two lines concern the parable of the physician.

Regarding the passage from "The mountain of Zhèn Róng vibrates" to "Jū Mào": this refers to the first [section]. The "Parable of the Medicinal Herbs" chapter precisely clarifies the appearance in the world and the preaching of the Dharma according to the desires [of beings].
"Róng" means clarity; "Xiù" means to stand out prominently. The physical body (*rūpakāya*) of the World-Honored One is as radiant as a mountain of gold.
Because he appears within the great trichiliocosm for the sake of benefiting and bringing joy [to beings], the Sūtra says: "The color of the Tathāgata’s body is like a mountain of gold. This is it.
Regarding its meaning: *teng* (騰) means to surge; *wei* (委) means to flow out or discharge. The waters of the myriad streams flow eastward into the ocean;
hence it is so called. The "ocean" is a metaphor for the Buddha’s wisdom. It refers to the manifest teaching of the Dharma-gate, which flows abundantly into the ocean of the Tathāgata’s wisdom.
As for "eighty thousand," this is a rounded figure for eighty-four thousand; it mentions the larger number, and thus says "eighty thousand. It is also like... [text continues].
The *Abhidharmakośakārikā* states: "The Muni taught eighty thousand aggregates of Dharma. Furthermore, the "Treatise on the Arts" (*Yishu*) in the *Hanshu* says:
"Regarding the 'Three Hundred [Odes],' their actual number is three hundred and six pieces. As for those that have been omitted, it is as the *Shujing* says:
'If one wishes to examine the great ocean, one must first examine its source. The 'source' refers to the origin of the water; thus, the source is used as a metaphor for the fundamental."

The great ocean is a metaphor for the subsequently attained wisdom (*pṛṣṭhalabdha-jñāna*). Just as the waters of the great ocean originate from a remote source, the Tathāgata’s subsequently attained wisdom arises from the fundamental [wisdom].
From this subsequently attained wisdom, he expounds eighty-four thousand Dharma-gates; thus it is said. This interpretation is excellent and is entirely appropriate for the wise.
"Tín" (津) means to cross over. Thus, in the *Lunyu* (Analects), when Zilu asked about the ford (*tín*), the commentary states: "A ford..."
"Crossing over" (*du*) refers to the act of ferrying across. This signifies that each of the eighty thousand dharma-gates possesses the meaning of being a distinct means of salvation.

Regarding "overhanging clouds" (*aidai*): the *Guangya* states that "dai" is like "yi-hui"; "yi-hui" describes the appearance of clouds rising in dense profusion. The *Tongsu Wen* states that when clouds cover [the sky], it is called "aidai."

"Shelter" (*piyin*) refers to protection; "sudden" (*zòu*) refers to rapidity. Yet, when clouds arise in dense masses, sweet rain must surely fall. This serves as a metaphor for the Buddha’s compassion having already been manifested:
it provides great shelter for all living beings, and its benefits extend widely from the three types of grasses and two types of trees down to the lowest levels.

The commentary states: "As for 'because of being young merchants' (up to) 'the city of transformation,' this is the second section. As for 'as for because of,' it is a term used to introduce the subject.
'Young' means small. 'Merchants' refers to those who trade. 'Wearied' means exhausted and indolent. 'Distant' refers to a long journey. 'Perilous' refers to obstacles and difficulties."
"Shi" (始) means "the beginning. "Xun" (循) means "to follow in accordance with. Thus, the *Lunyu* says: "The Master was *xunxunan* (循循然). Zheng Xuan explained: "*Xun* means 'to accord with';
'youdao' (誘導) means 'to guide. The meaning is evident and shall be examined below.
"Shu Ya zi wan yu (to) you jia zhe. This is the third section. "Zhi" means young; "wan" means to enjoy or favor. "Xian xuan":
according to the *Yupian* (entry 5-xian, qú-yán second tone), we take the initial reading here. The *Shuowen* writes it this way. "Shù xián qiè" and "yáng qiè" mean a wild goat.
The *Erya* states that a sheep reaching six chi in height is called a "xian," just as a horse of eight chi is called a "chong. Guo [Puzi].
Zhu Puxu’s commentary states: According to the *Rites of Zhou*, horses eight chi or taller are called *long* (dragons); oxen seven chi tall are called *cháng* (pronounced as in *rǒngjūn*);

and oxen five chi tall are called *yáng*. The character *cháng* is pronounced *zhì*; the character *yáng* is pronounced *fǎng-xī*. Dogs four chi tall are called *áo*; chickens three chi tall are called *kūn*. The character *kūn* is pronounced *kūn*.
The *Yùpiān* says that on Mount Qiánlái there is a creature with the body of a sheep and the tail of a horse; it is described as a beast-bird. Its... [text fragment].
It has the form of a sheep with a horse’s tail; it is called the *xián* (wild sheep). Today there is the country of the Great Yuezhi, where there are large sheep with donkey tails.
*Jìng* means completion; it also means illumination. It is also written as *zhào*, which likewise means brightness. Taking the former [reading] as correct.

*Jìn* means to advance, as in the *Jin* hexagram of the *Zhou Yi*. With *Kun* below and *Xī* above, the *Tuan* of the *Jin* hexagram says: "Jin means advancing. Brightness emerges from above the earth."
Therefore it is said: "The *qiú* (犪)"—according to the rhyme of *zhǔnlì*—is written as *yōu* (龍, with the phonetic *qú* and *zhuī*). Its character is composed of the radical for "ox" (*niú*).

It is like *zhāo* and *shào* (the latter pronounced *sān* and *qú*, *zhuī*, and *wú*). Furthermore, in the *Shuowen Jiezi*, the *Yupian*, and other such works, there is no instance of reading *rǎo* as *dá*.
Someone has cited the *Zhuangzi*, which says: "The *kuí* pitied the *xián*. The *kuí* said to the *xián*: 'I move by hopping on a single leg. This refers to that one leg.
The ox travels a thousand *li* in a single day. The reason we know this is that the subsequent scripture states:
"Its speed is like the wind. Furthermore, the *Shanhai jing* says: "In the Eastern Sea there is Mount Liuyan. There is a beast there resembling an ox, with a grayish body and no horns.

Whenever it emerges from or enters the waters, there will surely be wind and rain. Its radiance is like that of the sun and moon, and its voice is like thunder. Its name is Kui. The Yellow [Emperor]...
The Emperor obtained it and made a drum from its hide; its sound was heard five hundred *li* away, and he used it to awe the world.

In the two preceding passages, the character is written simply as *kui*. However, according to the *Erya*, the "ox with a fish-like head" (*yu wei fan*) is the *gou* ox; Guo Pu states that this is the same as the *you* ox.

The *yǒu* (pronounced with the *chén* and *bēi* finals) is like an ox but larger; its meat weighs several thousand *qīn*. It originates from within Shǔ. The *Shānhǎijīng* states: "Mount Kuí has many *yǒu*-oxen.
Following the *Yǐyá*, this character for *yǒu* was originally written as such. Today, however, it is transmitted as the character *yǒu* (牛憂).
This is an error by those who transcribed the text.
The commentary states: "From this, he crushes the ten armies... [down to] the bright pearl. This is the fourth section. Regarding the "ten armies," the *Saṃyukta-piṭaka-sūtra* (*Zàzàng jīng*) says:
desire, sorrow, hunger, impurity, craving, spittle, sleep, fear, doubt, and poison; as well as fame and profit, self-exaltation, and contempt for others—these shall be explained below.
The *Erya* says: "Hou" means "ruler. Furthermore, it is said that the "ten armies" refers to the ten afflictions (*kleśa*).

This is also [the case], yet it does not reach the previous interpretation. As for the statement in the commentary (*shu*) that "the teaching texts have not been seen to speak of ten afflictions as the Ten Armies," this refers to the fifth section, which extends from "establishing the eight truths" (*ba di*) to "wondrous medicine. Regarding the eight truths:

there are four truths each for both the conditioned (*saṃskṛta*) and the unconditioned (*asaṃskṛta*), and thus they are called the eight. The text below will explain this itself, so there is no need to elaborate further here. Question: How does the *Śāstra* judge this sutra?
There are seven parables in total. Why are only five cited here in this commentary? The answer is that the intent of the treatise is to remedy those with seven types of pride;

therefore, it explains all seven parables in general. As for why only five are given here, it is because these two—the "Infant" and the "Son of a Poor Man with a Tied Jewel"—are parables concerning the realization of the middle and lower-grade *śrāvakas*, and thus they are not explained here. Alternatively...
It says: "The intent of this preface is merely to discuss the general purport of the sutra; why must it be cited in full? Therefore, it is not explained.
Although this judgment is made, the previous interpretation is superior, as it possesses profound significance. Let those who are discerning examine it in detail.

"Adorning [the text] so as to flourish for a thousand ages": this refers to the section on "generally manifesting superior capability," where first the superiority is directly manifested and then illustrated by a metaphor;

this is the initial part. "Adorning" (*zǎo*) refers to the literary style. According to the *Yùpiān*, it is pronounced *hú*; other readings are *zhān* or *zhān* (with the second tone), meaning "brilliant.
If following the original *Shuowén*, it is pronounced *shū* (with the fourth tone); tradition says it means "to cover. The intent is to show that the phrasing of this sūtra is skillful.

Regarding the character *yàn* (棪): it appears in various scriptures as follows, such as in the *Jìrán xiánjū* (寂然閑居) and other texts. Scholars deeply admired its elegance and artistry, and through this, they conceived faith in it.
As the script states, "Ān ān yàn tiān chí" (摛摛棪天遲), this refers precisely to that matter.

My former teacher said that it is pronounced *yú zhān* (餘瞻); the meaning is that of flying upward, like a flame surging upward. Furthermore, in Sima Xiangru’s *Zǐxū fù* (子虛賦), it is used to express lofty virtue and intention.
The Son of Heaven heard it being recited; hence it is called "Unfolding the Celestial Court. "Profoundly transcending the hundred schools" (sù yì bǎi zōng zhī wài): "profound" (sù) means deep;
"transcending" (yì) is pronounced tú jié (with the second character read as yù). This indicates that the meaning of this sutra is profound and far-reaching, surpassing the various hundred schools.

"The hundred schools" refers to the fundamental tenets of the hundred schools. "Encompassing the seven stages while standing alone in glory among the nine divisions": [this describes its superiority].
The "seven stages" refer to the seven stages beginning with the lineage (*gotra*). The "nine divisions" refer to the ninefold canon of the Hīnayāna.
These seven stages and nine divisions—extending from below as measured by the ruler—are crowned by the five vehicles, standing alone preeminent throughout the ages.

The "five vehicles" refers to the three vehicles together with humans and devas; alternatively, it is said to include the indeterminate and those without nature (*agotra*). "Preeminent" (*ying*) means outstanding and brilliant. Therefore—
The *Shangshu* says: "The auspicious grain has ears growing together.

The commentary states: "How great it is! (extending to) "the myriad phenomena. This establishes a metaphor below to illustrate what is within. First, the fundamental principle is directly presented; later, a metaphor is established for illustration.
This is the first [part]. "How great it is! is a term of praise. "One reality" refers to the One Vehicle (*ekayāna*). The two... [text ends]
"Those of expedient means" refers to the followers of the Two Vehicles.

Regarding the phrase in the Commentary, "How could one use the dark waters of the Míng [to convey this]?"—this is an illustration by way of analogy. "Míng" refers to the ocean. As the *Zhuāngzǐ* says:
"In the Northern Míng there is a fish; in the Southern Míng, the Heavenly Pond. "Miaogao" (妙高) is called *Sumeru* in Sanskrit; here it is translated as "Wondrous High."
"High" (*gāo*) means "squarely comparable. "Jùn" (峻) means "lofty. "Zhú" (躅)—pronounced *zhílù*—means "to tread upon"; it refers to a "trace" or "footprint. The intended meaning is as follows:
although the ocean is deep, it cannot be compared to the profound purport of this sutra; although the mountain is lofty, it cannot be likened to the exalted clarity of this sutra.
In its great essence, it is higher than Mount Sumeru and deeper than the vast ocean. The above constitutes a general and specific manifestation of the fundamental tenets of the sutra.
The commentary begins by stating "The Wondrous Dharma" (up to) "all collectively named. From here below is the formal explanation of the title.

Within this, there is first a general explanation and subsequently a detailed analysis. Of these, the former first explains the collective name of the entire work, and the second explains the specific designation of each chapter;
this is the first part. "Maha" means vast and grand. "Dhvaja" means a banner or standard, such as a military ensign used to signal a host of troops. This present title is likewise so designated.

"Marking the various meanings of the sutra" (the character *jing* [pronounced *qing* or *ying*, meaning "to manifest" or "to indicate") refers to the preface of the first chapter (*pin*) up to the specific headings. This explains the individual titles of the chapters;

just as a mirror can reflect forms, by observing the chapter one immediately understands its subject matter. "Manifesting the distinctions of the means" (*quan*)—the term "heading" (*mu*) refers to the specific name of each chapter.

"From 'The Commentary on the Profound Meaning of the Lotus Sutra' (Shu yin han chi gui) to 'Manifesting the Lotus'": This is the separate explanation. Within it, the first part is the separate explanation of the title;

the second part explains the meaning of the sutra and the names of its chapters. Regarding the first part, there are two sections: first, the direct explanation of the title; second, the clarification that the Dharma of the sutra is beneficial for sentient beings.

Within the first of these, there are again two parts: first, the separate explanation of the dharma and the metaphor; second, the comparative analysis of the dharma and the metaphor. This is the first [of those]. The Dharma...
Regarding the term "dharmas as both norms and supports" (*dharmāḥ samāśritāḥ*): this is an explanation of the meaning of *dharma*. There are two senses of *dharma*:

first, support (*āśraya*), and second, norm (*vidhi*). Support means not abandoning one's own nature; norm means that which can produce understanding in sentient beings. Thus, the *Vijñaptimātratāsiddhi* states: "Dharma means norm and support;
'norm' refers to the standard of conduct, and 'support' refers to upholding. Here, *dharma* encompasses both meanings; hence it is so described.

"Binding all auspicious signs to express the wondrous" explains the character *miao* (wondrous). "Binding" (*wan*) means to tie or connect. "The flowers are both exquisite and blooming" explains the character *hua* (flower).
In discussing the interpretation of the lotus flower (*padma*), there are two meanings: first, emerging from the water; second, blossoming.
Here, "exquisite" (*xiu*) refers to emerging from the water, and "blooming" (*fa*) refers to blossoming. "To manifest the lotus by combining all these beauties" explains the character *lian* (lotus).

The essence (*tǐ*) and function (*yè*) are both presented; the phenomenon (*fǎ*) and the metaphor (*yù*) are raised together. This constitutes a comparative analysis through the correspondence of the subject (*yǒu fǎ*) and the metaphor.

"Essence" refers to the intrinsic nature (*tǐxìng*); "function" refers to the efficacy (*yònggōng*). The *Sūtra of Immeasurable Meanings* discusses the intrinsic nature, while the *Lotus Sūtra* clarifies the efficacy.

Regarding the raising of both phenomenon and metaphor: the "Wondrous Dharma" (*mìofǎ*) is the phenomenon, and the "lotus flower" (*liánhuā*) is the metaphor. Since this sūtra takes both phenomenon and metaphor as its title, they are said to be raised together.
"Regarding the passage [from] 'the paths of the Half and the Full' [to] 'now clearly manifest': this clarifies that the Dharma of the sutras benefits sentient beings.

'Half' refers to the Two Vehicles; 'Full' refers to the Mahāyāna. Therefore, the Sutra says: 'For the sake of the śrāvakas, I preach the Dharma of half-syllables; for the sake of the bodhisattvas...'"

Regarding the statement that "the path of taking and abandoning is precisely what is emphasized": this scripture’s primary tenet clarifies that the One Vehicle (Ekayāna) is the reality and the Two Vehicles are provisional.
It causes one to abandon the two provisional vehicles and take up the one reality. "Emphasized" (zhuo) means made clear.
"Those who comment on the sūtra [state] 'it is permanent'... up to 'this is the reality. This section below explains the sūtra and the title of the chapter.

Within it, first the name of the sūtra is explained, and subsequently the reason for the chapter's title is clarified. Regarding the explanation of the sūtra’s name, there are two parts: first, a general enumeration; second, a specific explanation of this [sūtra]. This is the first part.

Regarding the passage from "The constant is the track of the Way" to "reaching the shore of awakening": within this specific commentary, there are first four phrases that cite and explain the title of the sutra, followed by two phrases that clarify the intent of preaching the sutra.
From "The constant is the track of the Way" to "the common folk": this cites and explains the title of the sutra. "Common folk" refers to ordinary beings (*pṛthagjana*).
They are called "common" because they are perpetually deluded and reject true knowledge; it is intended that they may ultimately achieve liberation.

"Reaching the shore of awakening" clarifies the intent of expounding this sutra; it is a hope, and it is the ultimate goal. "The ford of suffering" refers to the cycle of birth and death within the three realms.
"Sutra" means to investigate to the ultimate limit. "The shore of awakening" refers to the fruit of Buddhahood.

Thus, when the Buddha preaches the Dharma, he hopes to cause sentient beings to ultimately leave behind this ford of the suffering of birth and death and, in the end, ascend to the other shore of the fruit of Buddhahood.

The preface to the commentary (*shù*) means "origin" (*yóu*). The phrase "therefore it is called the first" explains the title of the chapter. Regarding "the preface (*xù*) means 'origin' (*yóu')": this explains the character *xù*.
Regarding "a chapter (*pǐn*) means 'category' (*lèi')": this explains the character *pǐn*. It refers to the branching out of streams from a pond.
"Hui" (彚) means "to gather together," which refers to categories (*jāti*). "Di" (第) means "order" or "sequence. "Deng" (等) explains the two characters "di-yi" (第一), meaning "first.
When it says "the sūtra contains twenty-eight categories," etc., this is a comprehensive explanation of the term "first."

Regarding the commentary’s first section, “To repay the cause” (extending to) “to manifest the timing and capacity,” this introduction to the arising of the sutra contains five general meanings. Briefly stated, the general purport is as follows:
namely, repaying oneself and repaying others; generating faith and generating understanding; bestowing the fruit and bestowing the cause; present benefit and future benefit;
and [the teachings] regarding the Dharma and regarding persons. These correspond respectively to the five [meanings]; they may be understood by reflecting upon them.

In the commentary, from the initial "repaying the cause" (至) up to "repaying the cause of the teaching," the subsequent section explains the repayment of the cause. This passage consists of three parts: first, listing the six reasons;
second, citing the names and defining their characteristics; this [section] is the first.

The commentary states: "The fruit of Buddhahood cannot be achieved in vain" (up to) "the six meanings. This generally clarifies the reason for the sequence of the six causes. First is the analysis; second is the conclusion.

Regarding "the fruit of Buddhahood cannot be achieved in vain," this refers to the cause of practice (*pratipatti-hetu*). Regarding "practice does not arise in isolation; it must be sustained by aspiration (*praṇidhāna*)," this refers to the cause of aspiration.

Regarding "although practice and aspiration may arise of their own accord," this refers to the cause of seeking (*paryeṣaṇā-hetu*). Regarding "even when encountering conditions," this refers to [the cause of attainment].

"Maintaining the cause so that the attainment of the fruit is perfected" refers to the cause of characteristics (*lakṣaṇa-hetu*). "The great characteristics being manifest" refers to the cause of explanation (*deśanā-hetu*).
"By this, one repays the cause" is the conclusion, summarizing these six meanings. Therefore, it can be understood as such; there is no need for further separate explanation.

Regarding the commentary’s response concerning the "causes of activity" (*pravṛtti-hetu*): the following section cites the names and distinguishes their characteristics. Now, each of these six causes possesses two aspects:

first, the citation of scriptural texts to demonstrate them; second, a general judgment and explanation thereof. Within the section on the causes of activity, the portion from the beginning up to "it should be known" (*jñātavyam*) below consists of the cited scriptural passages.
"Once the Dharma of all Buddhas has been fully practiced"—this is the general judgment and explanation; what follows below is all analogous, as shall be evident from the text itself.

Regarding the phrase "one should know" in the *Fangbian pin* (Expedient Means) section of the commentary, it is a citation of the scriptural passage. Furthermore, some say that [the text] cites the eight profound [qualities].
The profound meaning [of this passage] is as follows: it takes the second [type of] practice as being profoundly deep; the remaining seven types follow by way of context.
Furthermore, it is said that all eight profundities are collectively cited to comprehensively clarify the response to practice. Why, then, does [the commentary] state that only the second is taken?

Examining this current interpretation, its reasoning is somewhat consistent and the textual meaning is roughly clear; thus, the previous explanation is superior. Regarding the absence of the sixth and eighth [types], there is no sixth.
"Unsurpassed. The eighth [point], the profound sustenance of what is not shared with śrāvakas and pratyekabuddhas, is that which the sutra treats briefly while the treatise explains extensively;
it should be understood as occurring below, namely, in the "Chapter on Expedient Means" (Upāya-paṭala).

The commentary from "The Dharma of the Buddhas" down to "because of the practitioner" provides a general judgment of the intent. The myriad practices cultivated are all causes for the knowledge of all modes;

it is only by fully performing these practices that one can attain Buddhahood. Now, as the fruit is fulfilled, this sutra is taught to repay those causal practices and, concurrently, to exhort others to cultivate them.
Thus, it clarifies that both self-benefit and the benefit of others are completely perfected.
The commentary’s response regarding "the cause of the vow up to the Buddha-body" is a citation of the source text. The *She shi* (Compendium of Explanations) states:
"As for the 'cause of the vow,' vows are manifold, yet they do not exceed two types. As the *Yogācārabhūmi-śāstra*, fascicle 48, says: 'There are two kinds of vows: first, the seeking of Bodhi.'"

The aspiration to benefit and bring happiness to others contains two aspects during the causal stage, but only one during the resultant stage; this is because once the fruit is perfected, there remains only the wish to deliver sentient beings.

Regarding the phrase "Just as I have previously aspired," the commentary states: Question: Since all four modes of birth are currently submerged in the nine realms of existence, and the fulfillment of the vow remains no different [from its initial intent], is this not a failure?
Answer: It is not so. The vow is that sentient beings may practice the causes and proceed toward the fruit just as I have done. Thus, it is born.
Having already resolved the mind and rejoiced in supreme enlightenment as the cause for entering the Way, one speaks of "fulfillment" in relation to those with whom there is a karmic connection;
thus, there is no error. Having already refuted various interpretations by summarizing them, what is presented here is solely the correct exposition.

All subsequent sections are of this same nature and will not be described at length again. Although the foregoing has already been detailed, it is now further clarified: when the Buddha made vows during his causal stage, he vowed to cause all beings...
"Birth is like my own practice of causes to realize the fruit; the Buddha has now perfected it. Because the fruit is already perfected, [some] say: 'Just as my former vows have now been fulfilled.
This does not mean that all sentient beings will simultaneously attain Buddhahood, which is what is meant by 'fulfillment.

Since it is said that one transforms all sentient beings and causes them all to enter the Buddha-way, we know that both [the cause and the fruit] are exhorted for practice and realization; it does not mean that all [will necessarily] attain it."

The name of the Buddha is "Fulfillment of Vows. Regarding the passage in the "Chapter on Lifespan" that says, "as for those who have attained the accomplishment of the Buddha-body," this refers to the generation of the mind [of awakening] at the stage of fruition, whereas previously one sought it through vows during the causal stage.
The subsequent citation and explanation merely speaks of "gathering" (*saṃgraha*); readers must understand this.

The commentary states, "If [it was] in former causal conditions... up to 'because of appearing in the world,'" which is the judgment of the intent. "If in former causal conditions" refers to the vow in the *Upāya-paryāya* (Chapter on Expedient Means).
"If in the present state of fruition" refers to the vow in the *Āyuṣ-pramāṇa-paryāya* (Chapter on the Lifespan).

Whether in cause or fruit, one must in all cases make a vow, praying that one's own body may likewise enter the Buddha-way. Now, in recompense for the preaching of this sutra, one should likewise cause sentient beings to make this vow.

"Because practice and vows correspond, one attains transcendence of the world. This is the general meaning. Suppose an external objection is raised: "In seeking the fruit of Buddhahood, one must rely upon cultivation.
Since the previous explanation of the causal practice is sufficient to lead to the attainment of the fruit, why is it necessary to further explain the cause that fulfills one's vows?
To this, the answer is given: "Because practice and vows correspond, one attains transcendence of the world. Question: How many kinds of vows are there? Answer: Indeed.
As for the aspiration that accords with causes, how could it have a fixed measure? Nevertheless, based on the sacred teachings, it may be briefly discussed.
For instance, according to the *Yogācārabhūmi-śāstra*, there are two types: first, seeking enlightenment; second, benefiting and bringing happiness to others.

Furthermore, various sūtras contain four great vows, such as those of Bhaisajyaguru (twelve), Amitābha (forty-eight), and the Avataṃsaka (one hundred and forty). There are many other varieties beyond these, which cannot be fully enumerated.

Question: What is the distinction between a vow (*praṇidhāna*) and a pledge (*pratijñā*)? Why are they mentioned together here? Answer: There is a slight difference between them. A vow is broad, while a pledge is narrow.
There are cases where there is a vow but not a pledge; this refers to merely giving rise to a single thought of aspiration without forming the resolve of a great pledge (*mahā-pratijñā*).

There are also cases where a pledge is itself a vow, such as making a pledge saying, "I shall practice with courageous diligence and never retreat," and so forth. Furthermore, it is like... [text continues]
The Bodhicitta Sūtra. There are ten vows and six mentalities of resolve. As for the ten vows:
first, I vow that all my roots of goodness shall be dedicated together with all sentient beings toward unexcelled bodhi.

Second, I vow that once I have dedicated them toward bodhi, by means of these roots of goodness, I shall always be able to make offerings to all Buddhas and never be born in a land where there is no Buddha.

Third, I vow that once I have been born in the lands of all Buddhas, I shall always be able to draw near to and attend upon them at their side, never being separated from the Buddhas for even a single moment.
Fourth, I vow that once I have drawn near to the Buddhas, they shall preach the Dharma for me, whereby I shall immediately attain the five supernormal powers (*pañcābhijñā*) of a bodhisattva.
Fifth, I vow that once I have attained these powers, I shall thoroughly penetrate the conventional truth of provisional names and understand the [first]...

First, may I attain the wisdom of the true Dharma. Second, having attained this correct wisdom, may I, with a tireless mind, preach it for the sake of sentient beings—teaching, exhorting, benefiting, and gladdening them—so that all may achieve understanding and liberation.

Third, having enabled sentient beings to achieve understanding and liberation, may I, through the spiritual power of the Buddha, go everywhere throughout the ten directions to make offerings, listen to the Dharma, and extensively gather in sentient beings. Fourth, may I, regarding all Buddhas...
Having received the True Dharma, may I be able to turn the wheel of the pure Dharma.
May all sentient beings of the ten directions who hear my teaching or hear my name abandon affliction and resolve to attain Bodhicitta.

Having made the ninth vow that I may cause the multitude to resolve upon Bodhicitta, may I always follow and protect them, removing what is unbeneficial and bestowing immeasurable happiness. May I sacrifice body, life, and wealth to gather and sustain the multitude.
Birth. To bear the True Dharma. Tenth: "May I, having borne the True Dharma, although practicing the True Dharma, have no mental activity, nor yet any non-activity;
for the sake of transforming sentient beings, may I not abandon my true vow. Regarding the six vows:
when a Bodhisattva resolves their mind, they first establish supreme sincerity and set forth a heart of resolute vows, never again succumbing to negligence, indolence, or laxity. Why is this?
One establishes a firm vow because it is sustained by five things: first, it can solidify the mind; second, it can subdue the afflictions (*kleśa*);

third, it can prevent negligence; fourth, it can destroy the five hindrances (*pañca-nīvaraṇa*); and fifth, it can diligently cultivate the six perfections (*ṣaṭ-pāramitā*). How does one establish this vow?
It refers to the practices from generosity (*dāna*) up to wisdom (*prajñā*). By means of the ten great vows, the Bodhisattva sustains the practice of the True Dharma. Six.
One must establish a great vow to restrain the heedless mind; thus one will certainly be able to practice with diligence, cultivate and accumulate the six perfections, and attain unexcelled bodhi.
Furthermore, the arousal of the bodhicitta must be endowed with ten virtues and three contemplations, which shall be explained below.

Moreover, as stated in the *Ajātaśatru-rāja-sūtra*, although the conditions encountered were the same, the results differed due to the power of their vows. It says: "In the past, immeasurable great kalpas ago..."

There was a Buddha who appeared in the world named Sarvābhibhū. He was traveling along a road with his disciples when three young boys saw the Buddha and his attendants, their radiance majestic and solemn.
They said to one another, "We should offer them our worship together. Two of the boys said, "Since we have no flowers or incense, with what shall we offer?
Then one of the boys immediately removed a white pearl from atop his head and offered it.
Taking them in his hands, he said to the two young children, "You may offer these as an offering. The two children also each removed their pearls and offered them to the Buddha.
One of the two said, "I do not dare to be like the Buddha; I wish to be like the Venerable One on the World-Honored One’s left side.
The other said, "I wish to be like the one on the right side. Another small child said, "I wish to attain the state of walking in the midst [of the assembly] like the Buddha. At that time...
After the three boys had made this vow, they each scattered their own jewels over the Buddha. Two resolved upon the mind of a śrāvaka;
their jewels remained on his two shoulders. One resolved upon the bodhicitta; his jewel remained above the Buddha’s crown and transformed into a jeweled canopy.
Within the canopy was a Buddha. The Buddha said to Śāriputra, "The one who vowed to be on the left is you. The one who vowed to be on the right is Maudgalyāyana."
It is so. "The one in between" refers to my own person. Because you all fear birth and death, you do not resolve to attain bodhicitta, desiring instead a swift nirvana.
For the sake of benefiting all sentient beings, I have extensively generated the supreme mind and thereby achieved buddhahood.
What has been cited above is intended to make this known; when it comes to the actual lecture, one should take only the essential points.

Regarding the commentary’s statement, “Because the Buddha in the past... [up to] ...seeks what is weighty,” this is the definitive judgment (*viniscaya*), which also serves to resolve external objections. The objection states: "It is logically sufficient that they mutually assist one another to attain the fruit; why, then, does it further speak of 'recompensing' and 'seeking' as causes? Therefore, this passage provides the explanation. Its meaning is as follows: * **Citation:** "In response to the request for causes" refers to the scriptural source. * **Definitive Judgment:** "Because the Buddha in the past... seeks what is weighty" establishes the final conclusion. * **Resolution of Objections:** It simultaneously addresses the following difficulty: "If it is simply a matter of mutual assistance for the sake of attaining the fruit, why is there mention of 'recompensing' and 'seeking' as causes? Thus, the text provides this clarification. Its significance is as follows: 1. **Recompense (*pratidāna*):** This refers to the repayment of the debt of kindness from past lives. 2. **Seeking (*prārthana*):** This refers to the aspiration for future results. 3. **Attaining Much (*bahu-lābha*):** This refers to the vast fruits of the path. These three aspects—recompense, seeking, and the attainment of much—are the meanings of the phrase "recompense, seek, and attain much. Furthermore, the term "much" (*bahu*) signifies the vastness of the merit and wisdom accumulated through the practice of the six perfections (*ṣaṭ-pāramitā*). Because these are vast, they are termed "much. The phrase "attaining much" indicates that by relying on these vast merits and wisdom, one attains the great fruit of Buddhahood. This is the meaning of the commentary's statement: "Because the Buddha in the past sought what is weighty, he now attains much. This explains the reason why the Buddha, having already attained the fruit, still speaks of "seeking" and "recompense. It is because he seeks the weighty causes of the past that he now attains the vast fruit; therefore, the scripture speaks of "recompense" and "seeking. Thus it is said. Therefore, regarding the phrase "now proclaiming," etc.: this present teaching is not merely a response to my own personal quest;
it is also intended to cause all sentient beings to give rise to a mind of respect and to seek [the Dharma] with reverence from virtuous friends. Question:

Does the account of seeking the sutra for the sake of the king precede or follow the periods of the sixteen princes and that of the Bodhisattva Never-Disparaging? Answer: I have not seen [a definitive sequence].
The text states: According to tradition, it is said that before he became king, he had not yet sought this sutra;
however, since the sixteen princes and the Bodhisattva Never-Disparaging had already sought this Dharma, his period as king should logically have preceded theirs. Furthermore, a question was asked:
Between this time when he was king and the time when he sacrificed his body to seek half a verse, which came first? The answer is: Sacrificing the body to seek the verse occurred even earlier.

Before the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka-sūtra* was sought, if one infers by means of reasoning, it ought to have existed previously. There are other such obstacles; one must apply this principle to resolve them.
Although the preceding analysis and interpretation may seem plausible at first glance, since there is no supporting evidence, it is difficult to determine the chronological order with certainty.
The commentary (*śāstra*) provides a response regarding the causes for upholding [the teaching], from [the phrase] "my body is this" onwards; this is a citation of the text.

First, concerning the reliance on Bodhisattvas who made offerings to Buddhas as numerous as the sands of five Ganges Rivers and so forth, *She* (Zhiyi) says: Question: Upon which stages or positions are these four reliances established? Answer: There are many traditional explanations. One says:

The stage prior to the path of seeing (*darśanamārga*) constitutes the first reliance, because one has not yet entered the state of an *ārya*. The first three stages constitute the second reliance, because they are common to the world.
The next four, five, and six stages constitute the third reliance, because they are common to the two vehicles (*śrāvaka* and *pratyekabuddha*). As for the remaining four stages...
This constitutes the fourth reliance, as it consists solely of bodhisattvas. Furthermore, the commentary by Paramārtha is as cited below in the sub-commentary (*śāstra*). Question:

According to the section on those who are in training (*śaikṣa*) and those beyond training (*aśaikṣa*), one must make offerings to Buddhas as numerous as the atoms in fifty worlds before attaining perfect enlightenment.

Why is the number [of worlds] here so small—only twenty-six *asaṃkhyeya-kalpas*? Answer: If one makes offerings to the Buddhas of one’s own land, twenty-six *asaṃkhyeya-kalpas* suffice. However, if this refers to other lands, the number is as follows:
Regarding the "Dust-World" (*rajas-loka*): it is also said that when one manifests supernatural powers to make offerings to the Buddha, there are fifty worlds.

If based on the power of karma, there are twenty-six *gaṅgā-nadī-vāluka* [eons], and furthermore, the lifespan increases by two hundred trillion years and so forth. Question: At the time when the eon increases, [the lifespan] reaches only eighty thousand years.
"Now why is it so numerous? He replied, "The four stages of the roots of goodness (catur-kuśalamūla) establish the Buddha-bodies and lands perceived by those who experience them;
this is because there are [four] sets of four continents (*cāturdvīpaka*). Their lifespans differ from those of ordinary beings. As the *Sāgaranāgarājaparipṛcchā-sūtra* states:

'At that time there was a Wheel-Turning King who ruled over sixteen sets of four continents. It is for this reason that the Bodhisattva, through what is induced during the two preceding stages, rules over and transforms these kingdoms."
The lands differ in their superiority or inferiority, and their lifespans likewise vary.

The phrase "therefore, at the time of passing away... [until] receiving and upholding" is an interpretive judgment. However, the preaching of this sutra does not merely respond to the maintenance of the Dharma;
it also exhorts sentient beings to constantly receive and uphold it.

The commentary’s response regarding the "mutual causality" (相因), up to the phrase "named the Lotus Sutra," is a citation of the text. As for the passage beginning with "Having already attained Buddhahood," some have distinguished six types of mutual causality in the response:
first, the external aspect (*bāhya-lakṣaṇa*), wherein he preaches Mahāyāna sūtras for the sake of the bodhisattvas;

second, the internal aspect (*adhyātma-lakṣaṇa*), wherein he enters the Samādhi of Immeasurable Meanings; third, the signless aspect (*animitta-lakṣaṇa*), wherein he rains down the four flowers; fourth, the ground aspect (*bhūmi-lakṣaṇa*), wherein he shakes the earth in six ways...
1. Moving; 2. Five distant characteristics; 3. Emitting light from the *ūrṇā* to gaze afar (some texts read "illuminate" [zhào] instead); 4. Six near characteristics.

Regarding those who, having seen these, give rise to doubt, eight characteristics are explained by adding two to the preceding [six]: 5. The fourfold assembly gazes upon him; 6. The eight classes of beings rejoice.
Although this explanation exists, the first six are preferable.
"Because the Buddhas of the three periods [of time] [relied upon] this sutra" is a general explanation; other sutras do not possess this. Regarding the "first major sign," the *She* (攝) states:

Question: What is the first sign? Answer: The auspicious omens such as the preaching of the *Anantamukha-dhāraṇī-sūtra* (The Sutra of Immeasurable Meanings) and entering meditative concentration are collectively termed the first sign.
If that were so, since the *Nirvāṇa Sūtra* is preached prior to the *Śeṣa-śāsana* (The Bequeathed Teaching), the *Nirvāṇa Sūtra* should be the beginning of the *Śeṣa-śāsana*.

Question: This is not analogous. It is not the case that the *Śāsanānuśāsanī* (The Bequeathed Teaching) is definitively taught only after [the Buddha’s] parinirvāṇa. Prior to the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka-sūtra*, the "Immeasurable" (*apramāṇa*) was already taught.

[Such] types are forever not vessels for the Mahāyāna. There are many other texts [on this subject], but fearing prolixity, they are not cited in full.
