According to the *Bieyi za ahan jing* (Separate Translation of the Ekottarika Āgama), the śramaṇa was an emanation, yet this had not yet been clearly distinguished; thus, regarding the ascetic practices of suffering and pleasure performed by the non-Buddhists, it was through the supernatural power of the devaputra that the charioteer was made to answer.
According to the *Yinguo jing* (Sūtra on Cause and Effect), when the Prince questioned the emanated bhikṣu, the bhikṣu answered for himself.
According to the *Puyao jing* (Lalitavistara Sūtra), he questioned the charioteer, and the charioteer gave a full account. These accounts correspond to the *Benxing jing* (Sūtra of Past Deeds).

If one follows the two aforementioned sūtras, the inclusion of questions and answers would be a mere superfluous arrangement; however, according to the *Lalitavistara*, such questions and answers present no obstacle.
May those possessed of wisdom take care to reflect upon this.
Regarding the observation made during the middle watch of the night concerning the musicians and others, the *Sūtra of the Previous Conduct* (*Pūrva-yoga-sūtra*) states:
While the Prince was in the palace sleeping at night, the devas of the Śuddhāvāsa heavens arrived at the city of Kapilavastu. At that time, all the people within the city became dazed and bewildered.
A certain son of heaven named Dharmacārin came to the palace and, by means of his supernormal powers, caused—
The various court ladies manifested all manner of hideous appearances, causing the Prince to give rise to a profound sense of weary detachment.
Then, the Devaputra Ghaṭīkāra, at the hour of midnight, addressed him, saying: "O Prince, may you now cause all devas and humans to abandon the world and go forth from home;
may you cultivate and study the Noble Path. Having heard this, the Prince departed from the palace, joined his ten fingers in palms-together salutation, and with a focused mind, recollected the One.
Having paid homage to all Buddhas and looked up toward the void, the Four World-Protecting Kings and others, knowing that the time for the Prince’s renunciation had arrived, all assembled together.
The devas raised a great cry, saying, "The time has now come; you who seek the supreme Dharma!"
"Do not remain here. The Prince reflected: "The time has now come for me; it is fitting that I go forth from the household life.
He immediately called his slave Chandaka, who was born on the same day as he, and said to him: "Quickly saddle my horse-king Kanthaka, who was born on the same day as I.
After being urged three times, Chandaka finally saddled Kanthaka. Then the Prince spoke to the horse: "This is now my final [departure]..."

He mounted [the horse] and did not mount again. At that time, there was a yakṣa in the air named Pāda, along with a host of other yakṣas, each supporting the four hooves of the horse with their hands as they proceeded slowly and steadily.
Chandaka said, "The palace gates have already opened. The Prince replied, "My mind is resolved and free from doubt. Having exited the palace gates, he reached the Vaiśālī gate.
There was a yakṣa named Śubhāvatī who, together with five hundred yakṣas, saw the Prince approaching. They said to one another, "The Prince is coming at midnight;
we should open the gates for him. After the yakṣa Śubhāvatī had opened the gates, the Prince departed from the city.
The devas of the desire realm each assumed the form of handsome māṇavas and stood before the Prince.

The son went before, leading the Prince along a level road. Brahmā and his retinue surrounded him on the Prince’s right side, while the hosts of the Trāyastriṃśa gods were on his left side; the Four Great Kings, the Gandharvas, and others likewise followed.
Holding his armor and staff, he walked before the Prince on the road. The devas in the void scattered flowers as an offering.
They traveled from midnight until the appearance of the morning star, covering two *yojanas*. According to the Mahāsāṃghika masters, they traveled twelve *yojanas*.
Other masters say they traveled one hundred *yojanas* until they reached a village named Mṛga-dāva at sunrise.
When he arrived at the dwelling of the seer Bhārgava, the gods of the Śuddhāvāsa heaven, neither too near nor too far from the Prince, manifested as a flower garland named Sumana beneath a tree.
There, they took the form of a barber holding a sharp razor and stood not far away. Having seen him, the Prince said to the barber, "Can you shave my hair for me?"
"No," he replied, "I can do it. He then used a sharp blade to shave the Prince’s hair—his invisible crown protuberance (*uṣṇīṣa*) and his deep-blue, spiral-tufted topknot.
At that time, Śakra, Lord of the Devas, caught the falling hair in his robe and took it away toward the heavens.
Having made these offerings and shaved his hair, he looked upon his body and saw that he still wore celestial robes.
He thought to himself, "These robes are not the garments of one who has left the household life. Who can give me a saffron-colored *kāṣāya* robe?
At that time, a deity from the Śuddhāvāsa Heaven, knowing the prince’s thoughts, transformed himself into a hunter wearing a *kāṣāya* robe and stood before the prince. Thereupon, the prince...
The Kāśika robes were worth billions of gold pieces and had been perfumed with various types of sandalwood and other fragrances;

having obtained these from a hunter in exchange for his own *kāṣāya*, and after sending Chandaka back, he took a blade in his own hand, cut his hair, shaved off his beard and mustache, and donned the *kāṣāya*.
According to the *Mahāprajñāpāramitā-śāstra*, he then mounted his horse and set out.
Twelve *yojanas*. As for the fourteen *yojanas* cited in the present commentary, there must be a different source; please examine this further.
Regarding Bhāgava, the *Annotated Mahāsāṃnipāta-sūtra* (Benxing jing zhu) states that he was a common master (*pāṣaṇḍin*) according to some accounts, while others call him Bhadraśreṣṭhin.
As for "on the banks of the Hiraṇyavatī River" and so forth, according to the *Mahāsāṃnipāta-sūtra*, he departed from Kapilavastu and traveled toward that [place] in Uruvilvā.

The village of Lumbinī was situated along the banks of the river. The Bodhisattva thought to himself, "Now, those sentient beings who seek liberation all practice various and manifold ascetic penances.
Having seen this, he resolved to perform a formidable and most extreme form of austerity.
There is a verse that says: When the Bodhisattva reached the Nairañjanā River, with a pure mind, he stood upon its bank.
He sat down. Because those seeking the Way were not yet true in their practice, he wished to undergo great austerities in order to transform those misguided followers.
The Bodhisattva further reflected: "In the world, there may be śramaṇas and brāhmaṇas who establish their practice by restricting their food, each maintaining purity.
Some of them eat only barley, or sesame, or small beans, or large beans—undergoing various forms of hardship."
The Bodhisattva thought to himself: "I too should act in this manner. Day by day, he took a single grain of black sesame, or a single grain of non-glutinous rice, or a small bean, and so on.
He continued in this way for six years. Becoming weary of that which was not the true path, he finally partook of milk-rice.
When the six years were completed, on the sixteenth day of the second month of spring, he acted as follows:
He thought: "I should not now realize enlightenment by means of such food. From whom else can I now seek exquisite food?
A certain devaputra, knowing the Bodhisattva’s mind, quickly went to the two daughters of the village headman Sujāta.
Upon arriving, he said to them: "You should know that the time has come; the Bodhisattva now seeks exquisite food, after which he intends to realize [enlightenment]."
“Anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi. You should now prepare for him sixteen portions of exquisite, fine milk-gruel.
Upon hearing this, the two women were filled with such joy and exultation that they could not contain themselves. They quickly gathered ten thousand cows and milked them;
the milk was then transferred to feed five hundred cows. On another day, they milked these five hundred cows and again transferred [the milk]...
The milk was drawn from two hundred and fifty cows; likewise from one hundred and twenty-five, sixty, thirty, and fifteen.
On the following day, she milked these fifteen cows and placed their milk with a portion of pure, high-quality non-glutinous rice to cook the milk-gruel for the Bodhisattva.
While those two women were cooking the milk-gruel, various signs appeared. At that time, the Bodhi...
"Sa. On the twenty-third day of the second month, at the time of dawn, having dressed in his robes with composure, he set out toward the village of Uruvilvā to beg for alms.

Gradually arriving at the village of Nandika, he stood silently outside the main gate of the village headman’s house, desiring to seek food. At that time, the two daughters of the village headman, Sujāta..."
He took a single golden bowl, filled it to the brim with milk-rice mixed with honey, and placing it before the Bodhisattva, held it with his own hands and said:
"I pray that you will accept this milk-rice mixed with honey from me. The Bodhisattva asked:
"To whom shall I give this bowl after I have eaten? To whom shall I entrust it later? The woman said, "Entrust it to you, O Noble One.
The Bodhisattva said, "For such a vessel as this, there is no cause or occasion [to receive it]. The woman said, "Noble One, do as you please; reflect upon what should be done.
Having accepted it, the Bodhisattva went to the banks of the Nairañjanā River. Upon arrival, he placed the food he had received on a clean spot and removed [his upper garment].

He entered that river with his robes to bathe. As the Bodhisattva was bathing, the devas in the void sky mixed various subtle and wonderful fragrant powders with the water and rained down a variety of scents upon the surface of the water.

Once the Bodhisattva had finished bathing and wished to cross the water, the current was so swift and rapid that he was unable to get across. At that time, there was a great tree on that river named Aṭa.
"Who is this? [The Bodhisattva asked. "It is the deity of that tree, named Kāpota (meaning 'Little Peak').

At that time, the deity, with arms adorned with various necklaces and ornaments, led the way toward the Bodhisattva. Then the Bodhisattva took the hand of the tree deity and successfully crossed over that river."
When the Bodhisattva had finished eating that gruel, he cast the golden bowl into the river and proceeded toward the Bodhi tree to receive the auspicious grass (*śālistamba*).
The *Sūtra on Past Deeds* (*Pūrva-yoga-sūtra*) states: The Bodhisattva thought to himself, "In order to realize the state of a Bodhisattva, upon what seat should I sit?
He immediately realized for himself that he should sit upon grass. At that time, the devas of the Śuddhāvāsa heaven addressed him, saying, "It is so, it is so."
"It is so. All past Buddhas sat upon seats of grass. The Bodhisattva reflected, "Who can provide me with some?
At that time, Śakra, the King of the Trāyastriṃśa Heaven, immediately transformed his body into that of a grass-cutter and stood before the Bodhisattva, cutting grass.
The Bodhisattva went up to the man and asked, "What is your name? He replied, "My name is Kṣemaṅkara."
Having heard this, the Bodhisattva thought to himself: "I now desire to seek my own welfare; let me first seek welfare for others.
I shall certainly realize and attain Bodhi. The Bodhisattva said, "Will you give me some grass? At that time, the grass-cutter immediately offered him the grass.
The Bodhisattva took it and went beneath the Bodhi tree. Furthermore, according to the *Caoyin jing* (Sutra on the Causes and Conditions), it is named...
For the sake of auspiciousness: as for the Vajrāsana, it is one hundred paces wide.
According to the second fascicle of the *Mahāprajñāpāramitā Sūtra*, wherever the Tathāgata travels, there is naturally a Vajrāsana; otherwise, the Buddha’s body would sink into the earth.
Regarding the subduing of the Māra army: when the Bodhisattva was proceeding toward the Bodhi tree, he gave rise to this thought:
"Within this realm of desire, that King Māra Pāpīyān is the sovereign. I must now speak to him so that he may know [my intent].
If I do not inform him, I shall not achieve Great Enlightenment. Why is this? It is because I wish to subdue that Māra Pāpīyān, to bring him under my influence, and furthermore—"

He gathers and subdues all the devas of the desire realm. Within those māra hosts and their palaces, there are further immeasurable and boundless māra retinues and devas who have planted various roots of goodness in the past;
upon hearing that he has realized awakening, they all come forth and resolve to attain bodhicitta. Having reflected thus, the Bodhisattva, from between his eyebrows...
From within the mark of the white tuft of hair, he emitted a single ray of light named "Able to Subdue and Disperse the Multitudes of Mara’s Armies.
Having emitted this light, it immediately reached the palace of Māra at that very moment, eclipsing all the light of the ancient palaces and the karmic power of all those Māras.
Furthermore, this light spread laterally throughout the trichiliocosm, creating a great radiance that filled it entirely.
At that time, Pāpīyas, while asleep, was suddenly startled in his heart and naturally saw inauspicious signs in a dream.
Awakening from sleep, his entire body trembled and his mind was ill at ease. He summoned all the members of Māra’s household and commanded them to assemble, saying:
"O you all, having seen an inauspicious dream, I am filled with great terror.
It is not long before I shall surely lose this place; I fear that someone of even greater majesty, power, and merit may come to be born here."
In that place, acting as my representative, there was a yakṣa named Gandhamṛga who guarded that Bodhi tree.
Not far away, seeing the Bodhisattva approaching, he immediately informed a companion named Raktākṣa Yakṣa, saying:
"O worthy one, quickly go to the side of Māra on my behalf and deliver these words: 'Formerly, Krakucchanda and...'"
In this very place where the noble Anāgāmins, along with Kāśyapa and other great celestial seers and sages,
attained perfect enlightenment, there now dwells another person of great diligence, endowed with all the marks of excellence, who has encroached upon the realm of Māra;
he is the son of King Śuddhodana of the Śākya clan, named Siddhārtha, who has already abandoned ascetic practices.
He has come here. May Your Majesty know that the time has arrived. Having heard this, Red-Eye quickly went to the abode of Pāpīyān and related it as described above.

Upon hearing this, the Māra King immediately summoned the gods of Paranirmita-vaśavartin, Nirmāṇarati, Tuṣita, the Trāyastriṃśa, and the Cāturmahārājika heavens, along with all the nāgas, yakṣas, up to the mahoragas, kumbhāṇḍas, rākṣasas, and piśācas.
Śakra and the others were commanded, saying: "All of you, assemble and listen to my instructions.
There is one of the Śākya clan who desires to attain bodhi; let us go together to him and sever such a courageous resolve."
"Do not allow him to attain realization. Thereupon, he arrayed four kinds of elite troops, clad in armor and bearing weapons.

Furthermore, there were immeasurable hundreds of thousands of millions of billions of celestial and demonic armies, capable of manifesting various terrifying forms. This host of soldiers set out immediately upon receiving their orders.
The Demon King addressed the assembly of yakṣas, saying: "You all should reduce your numbers and proceed swiftly to the Bodhi tree."
They hid themselves beneath the trees and remained there, lest any of the Śākya clan should be in this vicinity.
At that time, the yakṣas stayed hidden not far from the trees; when they saw the Bodhisattva approaching from afar, his body was resplendent like a mountain of gold.
It radiated light so brilliantly that it was beyond all comparison. Having heard the report from the tree deity, they all scattered in every direction and fled.
The Māra King said to the Bodhisattva, "It is not fitting for you to remain beneath this tree. Why?
Because there are many piśācas, yakṣas, and rākṣasas here who constantly come to devour men. The Bodhisattva replied, "My mind is without fear, nor is it—"
"You lack wisdom. However, I have long known that in the past, various Buddhas attained the Noble Path beneath this very tree;
it is for this reason that I have come here. Then a yakṣa said to the Bodhisattva, "You should quickly move elsewhere.
The Bodhisattva replied, "I wish to attain bodhi right here. At that time, the yakṣa addressed the Māra King, saying, "Please act further..."
"What can be done to make him depart? Pāpīyān replied, "Only by various skillful means should he not be permitted to remain here.
Having seen Māra speak these words, the Bodhisattva spread grass and sat down, making this aspiration:
"I now sit upon that adamantine place where all the Buddhas of the past have sat. Having sat here, I shall subdue the King of Māras and sever all [afflictions]."
"Afflictions! You shall realize the subtle, wondrous, ambrosial, and refreshing Dharma. At that time, the Māra king vanished from that spot, concealing his body so it was no longer visible;
after a short while, he manifested his form again with disheveled hair and soil covering his entire body.
Wearing a garment of deerskin, with parched lips and a sunken face, he appeared as if hungry and thirsty; in his hand, he held a large bundle of books.
He came swiftly and, approaching the Bodhisattva, cast the letter he held into the Bodhisattva’s presence. The River spoke thus:
"This one letter was sent by you, of the Śākya clan, through Mānava;
this one is from Nirūḍha; this one is from Citra; this one is from Nanda; this one is from Ānanda."
"Nanda, these various other books were each sent to you by those young Śākya princes.
The writings upon them are forged, untrue, and filled with false and deceptive words, stating: 'Devadatta is now here in this city of Kapilavastu;
having received the royal throne, he has entered your palace and has taken possession of everything belonging to you.'"
"The queen and consorts have taken your father, Great King Śuddhodana, and cast him into prison.
Furthermore, your uncles—Śuklodana, Droṇodana, and Amṛtodana—as well as all the other Śākya kings, have been driven out and banished beyond the city walls.
Upon seeing this letter, you must come at once. Having heard this, the Bodhisattva reflected that the realms of the world are entirely impermanent.

It is defiled and impure; arising and ceasing from moment to moment, it does not abide for even an instant. Having reflected thus, he made this vow: "I shall not attain the Way until I rise from this seat.
Māra then addressed his hosts of armies, saying: "All of you, unify your minds; do not be startled, do not be afraid."
"Do not fear; do not flee. I am merely testing their minds. He then addressed his daughters, saying, "Each of you must listen to my words.
You should go to that son of the Śākyas and observe his mind to see whether he possesses any lustful desire.
Having received their father’s command, the māra-daughters arrived at that place and, not far from the Bodhisattva, manifested all manner of seductive charms.
[He observed] the Bodhisattva’s profound mind in tranquil concentration, inherently pure and stainless, with his sense faculties well-restrained and his mind thoroughly subdued.
Having seen this, [the son] felt shame and returned to his father’s presence to report his own inability.
Thereupon, the Māra-king went in person to where the Bodhisattva was and said: "For what reason have you come here? This place is filled with many evil dragons and clouds..."
"Rain falls and wild beasts roam; it is a place of fear and alarm. In the midst of the dark night, you have entered this forest alone and sit beneath these trees.
Are you not afraid of all those enemies, bandits, and thieves? The Bodhisattva replied:
"I now seek the peace of nirvāṇa, the path traversed by the Buddhas of the past. It is the supreme state of fearlessness, the end of all existence."
Because he was seeking this, he sat alone beneath this tree. Māra spoke to him again, saying: "Depart quickly from this place;

you shall certainly become a Wheel-Turning King (cakravartin), endowed with the seven treasures and ruling over all. Furthermore, your body is delicate and you have long remained within the deep palace;
now, in these wildernesses there are many solitary beasts, and I fear they may harm your person. Return to your own palace and receive [the pleasures of sovereignty]."
"The five desires delight the eyes and satisfy the mind; however, bodhi is difficult to attain, and [pursuing them] would only lead to weariness.
The Bodhisattva replied, "You need not speak such words now. Why is this? It is because my mind finds no pleasure in the affairs of the five desires.
I have long since renounced the places of abundance and joy within the four continents, as well as the seven treasures. Before long, I shall certainly attain it."
"Bodhi, you shall attain Buddhahood. Then the Māra King, employing further skillful means, addressed the Bodhisattva, saying:
"Arise quickly, arise quickly! Since your youth, you have never seen combat. The weapons of war are truly terrifying. When the Bodhisattva heard these words, he...
He remained resolute and would not comply. "I am now seated upon the adamantine firmness; sitting with legs crossed in the *paryaṅka* posture, I am extremely difficult to destroy.
Because I desire to realize that nectar-like Dharma, you, Māra King Pāpīyān, wish to act as you please.
Enraged, the Māra King spoke to the Bodhisattva, saying: "Why do you now, beneath this solitary tree, let out such hollow, roaring cries? You..."
Seeing the various troops of elephants, horses, chariots, and infantry under my command—a motley host of soldiers—I employed all manner of terrifying things against the Bodhisattva.
At that time, although the hosts of Māra exerted their full power, they could not cause even a single hair of the Bodhisattva to tremble.
The Bodhisattva spoke to the King of Māra, saying: "Listen well and attentively; I have come here to this Bodhi tree for the sake of primordial awakening."
He went down, took a handful of grass, spread it out, and sat upon it. Why was this?

He feared that at a later time he might become an enemy with Māra Pāpīyan, engaging in strife, contention, and harsh verbal abuse. "O Māra Pāpīyan, you have committed various evil deeds and possess no virtuous mind;
I now wish to sever all your enmity, O Māra Pāpīyan, and I wish to extinguish it."
"All you evil karmic forces: if I attain unsurpassed bodhi, I entrust all matters to you.
I pray that you will turn your minds [toward virtue] and give rise to great joy; may all the hosts of Māra be completely dispersed and defeated, fleeing in every direction.
Question: The *Avataṃsaka Sūtra* contains ten aspects (*lakṣaṇa*). I do not yet know how many of these are contained herein.

...as well. Regarding the answer concerning the ten marks: first, the mark of manifesting the relinquishing of celestial lifespan; second, the mark of manifesting birth, namely being born in a royal palace—these two are omitted here.
Third, the mark of manifesting as a youth; this begins from the passage "Having made this vow... and so forth. Fourth, the mark of manifesting as one who has gone forth [into homelessness];
this begins from the passage "Wandering out through the four gates... and so forth. Fifth, the mark of manifesting as one who practices austerities; [this occurs] at the *Hiraṇyavatī* River...

1. Below is the manifestation of the descent from the Tuṣita Heaven. 2. Below is the manifestation of entering the womb. 3. Below is the manifestation of birth. 4. Below is the manifestation of leaving home. 5. Below is the manifestation of practicing austerities. 6.

Below is the manifestation of approaching the Bodhi tree. This involves the rejection of what is not the path. 7. Below is the manifestation of subduing Māra. This is by means of wisdom. 8. Below is the manifestation of attaining supreme enlightenment through the realization of great bodhi, characterized by delighting in tranquil purity.
9. Below is the manifestation of turning the wheel of Dharma. This is at that time. 10. Below is the manifestation of entering nirvāṇa. This is one instance.

It is not said [here]. However, what is being clarified now is precisely the supramundane [attainment], not yet the entry into parinirvāṇa; therefore, the characteristics of entering parinirvāṇa are not discussed here.
Regarding the commentary’s passage from “Śāriputra and others requested” to “the fruit of the True and the Responsive”: Question:

For what reason do Śāriputra, Maitreya, Mañjuśrī, and the others differ in their requests concerning the object, the practice, and the fruit? Answer: Śāriputra is a lesser sage who has not yet been able to cultivate the One Vehicle (Ekayāna).
This is the Dharma. However, they merely cling to the notion that they are equal to the Tathāgata, not realizing that what they have attained is but a provisional means (*upāya*).

Therefore, Mañjuśrī asks about the object (*viṣaya*), desiring to know how to relinquish the provisional and grasp the real. Mañjuśrī possesses great wisdom and is able to practice the path of the One Vehicle; therefore, he asks about the practice (*caryā*).
Maitreya Bodhisattva has achieved the fruition and is destined to be born next in the rank of a Buddha; therefore, he asks about the fruition (*phala*). Thus it is.
There is a distinction. The *Shè* (Compendium) states: Question: When Śāriputra asks about the "object" (*viṣaya*), why are both the fruit and the cause explained?

[The text] reveals, shows, causes one to enter, and causes one to realize; the first three are the fruit, and the last one is the cause. Answer: Because they are the objects of wisdom (*jñāna*), they are provisionally termed "objects.
They are shown so that others may know them, thereby enabling them to cultivate and progress.

The Commentary refutes doubts (up to the phrase) "those with various doubts and regrets. The subsequent section on refuting doubts consists of three parts: first, clarifying the person who gives rise to doubt; second, revealing the reason why the doubt is removed;
and third, generally explaining and resolving difficulties. Within the first part, there is first a clarification of the doubting person, followed by a summary establishing the point.
Within that, first the Śrāvakas, then the Bodhisattvas. This is the first [of those]. Within this, there are two intentions; first, the Buddha’s own attainment of the Way.
"Until one reaches the point of never again becoming a Buddha"—this clearly explains the reason why the śrāvakas give rise to doubt. Second, "Therefore, Śāriputra...
until all doubts and regrets are severed"—this cites the scriptural text as proof.
Regarding the passage from "The various minor bodhisattvas" to "yet have no share": these are bodhisattvas. However, there are two types.
The first type doubts that other śrāvakas cannot become buddhas; the second type doubts that they themselves have no share in bodhi.
The commentary states, "By this, those of the three vehicles all possess the net of doubt," which serves as a concluding summary. Question:

Previously, when clarifying those who harbor doubts, only Śrāvakas and Bodhisattvas were mentioned, while Pratyekabuddhas were not. For what reason does the concluding statement say that people of all three vehicles equally possess doubt?
The answer to the previous statement regarding the śrāvakas and so forth includes the pratyekabuddhas as well; therefore, it concludes by stating that "both possess the net of doubt.

Furthermore, it may be that at the assembly of the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka-sūtra*, there were no individuals who had attained the fruit of a pratyekabuddha and thus removed their doubts to receive their prediction (*vyākaraṇa*);

for this reason, they were not cited previously. However, for those who sought that [fruit], it was taught to them as well. Thus, the concluding text applies equally to all three vehicles (*triyāna*). Nevertheless, within this category of doubt, it can be divided into four [types].
There are four categories: first, those who doubt themselves but do not doubt others, namely the followers of the Two Vehicles;

second, those who doubt others but do not doubt themselves, namely the Bodhisattvas of sudden enlightenment prior to the stages; third, those who doubt both themselves and others, namely the Bodhisattvas of gradual enlightenment prior to the stages;
and fourth, those who doubt neither themselves nor others, namely the Bodhisattvas on the stages. What is refuted here concerns only the first three.
The Commentary states: From the words of this sūtra up to "shall become buddhas," this reveals the reason for the removal of doubt.
It declares that there is no doubt regarding śrāvakas attaining buddhahood; this is said because they are those among the Buddha’s converts who are destined to attain it.
It does not mean that those of the two vehicles with fixed natures (niyata-gotra) will both attain buddhahood; such is the explicit intent of this sūtra, for it does not refute them.

The commentary [states], "In this section, from 'refuting doubt' to 'removing regret,' it explains away potential objections. The objection asks: "In the process of refuting doubt, is regret also refuted?
Therefore, the commentary explains: "The refutation of doubt herein also encompasses the aspect of refuting regret. How so? The commentary says:
"Formerly one regrets having practiced the Small Vehicle," and so on, up to "knowing that the Small is the cause for the Great. If this is so, why was it not explicitly designated [as such]?
The chapter speaks of destroying remorse.
The commentary states: "Doubt applies to all three vehicles" (up to) "...it does not say that the removal of remorse belongs exclusively to the Śrāvaka vehicle," referring to Śāriputra and others.

Regarding those of indeterminate nature among the two vehicles: prior to the preaching of the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka-sūtra*, they constantly regretted having cultivated the practices of the Lesser Vehicle and regretted realizing the fruits of the Lesser Vehicle.
Thus, their regret pertained only to the Lesser Vehicle. As for Bodhisattvas practicing the Mahāyāna, they originally did not study the Lesser Vehicle;

therefore, they have no such regret. That which is "broad" encompasses the narrow; because doubt extends throughout all three vehicles, it is called "broad. Because regret pertains only to the Lesser Vehicle, it is [called "narrow"].
This is narrow. Now, raising this point serves to dispel doubt and thereby subsume remorse; thus it is said. The Commentary states: Question:
Why does the Sūtra say that for those seeking the three vehicles, both doubt and remorse are severed? Answer: There are two explanations. First, the text is concise while the meaning is manifold;
they are spoken of together. In reality, a Bodhisattva cannot have remorse. Since the Great is superior and the Small is inferior, one cannot feel remorse toward that which is superior.

This refers to seeking the inferior. Second, it is said that there are also certain small bodhisattvas of indeterminate nature who perceive great bodhisattvas as being like a precipice, and thus retreat to seek a lesser station;
is this not regret? Although this principle exists, there is no explicit textual passage stating that one regrets cultivating the Great [Vehicle].

Yet, speaking from the perspective of ultimate truth, there is such a thing as regretting the cultivation of the Great [Vehicle]; hence the *Śraddhāparivarta* (Chapter on Faith and Understanding) says: "I regret having come here."
"I privately thought to myself: 'This might be the King,' and so forth, until: 'It would be better to go to that poor district where there is room to exert my strength.

Furthermore, for what reason have I come here? Based on these passages, it is clear that he repented his cultivation of the Mahāyāna. If this is so, why does the Master of the Commentary (*śāstrakāra*) say that there was no [repentance]?

Answer: The intent of the commentary is not to suggest that the Bodhisattva lacked repentance; however, such an instance did not occur during the assembly of the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka-sūtra*. This is the point of faith.
In the "Chapter on Understanding," in order to recount past events, it is asked: to what extent do the three grades of *śrāvakas* reach before they sever their doubts? The answer is:

as for the *śrāvakas* of superior capacity, in the past they had not heard the Mahāyāna and were not granted a prophecy (*vyākaraṇa*), thus harboring doubts that they lacked the potential to become Buddhas.

Now, having heard the Great Teaching and being granted the prophecy that they shall become Buddhas, their doubts are thereby removed. Thus, the subsequent scripture says: "Within the Buddha-lands of the ten directions, there is only..."

"The Dharma of the One Vehicle is equal," and so forth. It further says: "Since you have already known this... until the mind gives rise to great joy, knowing for yourselves that you shall become Buddhas.

After Śāriputra heard the Buddha’s teaching, at the beginning of the *Parable Chapter*, he leaped for joy and, immediately rising with palms joined, exclaimed, "I have attained what I never had before.
He further said: "Now, from the World-Honored One, I have heard what I have never heard before."
There was once a teaching that severed all doubts and regrets; today I finally know that you are truly the sons of the Buddha.
After the Buddha had thus confirmed this, he bestowed upon them their prediction of enlightenment. This is the place where those of superior faculties sever their doubts;

therefore, the subsequent sutra says: "Śāriputra, you should believe and accept the words of the Buddha. The speech of the Buddhas, the Tathāgatas, is without falsehood. Furthermore, a verse says: "All who seek the Three Vehicles..."

[The Buddha addressed] the people and others. Furthermore, when the Buddha arose from his meditative concentration, he spoke in verse: "Śāriputra, you should know that the words of all Buddhas do not differ," and so forth.
He further said: "All World-Honored Ones preach the path of the One Vehicle; now, this great assembly should all eliminate their doubts. He also said:
"Whether śrāvakas or bodhisattvas, upon hearing the Dharma I have taught... and so forth. He also said: "The twelve hundred..."

"The Arhats shall all likewise become Buddhas," and so forth. Furthermore, it says: "Since you have now understood that the Buddhas, the Teachers of the World, employ various skillful means according to what is appropriate, you should no longer harbor any doubts.
Your hearts will give rise to great joy, as you know for yourselves that you shall become Buddhas."

Among them, those of middling faculties, having heard the teaching on the burning house and the three vehicles, immediately attained realization. Once the Buddha had confirmed their understanding, he bestowed upon them the prediction of enlightenment (*vyākaraṇa*).
Thus the prediction says: "We, too, were likewise; we constantly reflected upon the faults of the Hīnayāna and did not know what we should do to attain the unsurpassed wisdom of a Buddha.
Although we heard the Buddha’s voice saying that we would become Buddhas, our minds still..."
Filled with anxiety and fear, he did not yet dare to eat. Only when he received the Buddha’s prediction would he find true peace and joy.

The Buddha granted him this prediction; immediately his doubts were dispelled. As for those of inferior capacity, upon hearing of the "transformed city," they attained realization within the "Chapter on the Five Hundred Disciples.
Once the Buddha had recounted and confirmed their prediction, and having received it, their minds attained realization, and they subsequently felt remorse and self-reproach. Therefore...
That chapter says: "World-Honored One, we have always harbored this thought, believing that we had already attained ultimate *nirvāṇa*.
Now we realize that we were like those lacking wisdom. It further says: "I now know for certain that I am indeed a bodhisattva, having received the prediction of *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*.
For this reason, I experience great joy, such as I have never known before."

There is. This refers to the point where those of inferior faculties sever their doubts. Question: Why is it that only those of superior faculties receive the prediction (*vyākaraṇa*) once their doubts are removed, while those of middling and inferior faculties do not?

Answer: Because their faculties differ in degree of excellence. Those of inferior faculties require the hearing of the prediction for their deluded sentiments to cease. Those of middling faculties are superior when compared to the inferior, yet are not as capable as those of superior faculties;

therefore, they too receive the prediction. Furthermore, they initially doubted the daytime [teaching], and their remorse extends throughout both the small and the great; these constitute the three grades.

"Are there also those who possess [such doubt]? The answer is: those of superior faculties do possess regret; this is fully set forth in the sutra itself. As for those of middling and inferior faculties, I shall now briefly point them out.
At the end of the *Nidāna-parivarta*, it says: 'Those seeking the three vehicles, if they have any doubts or regrets,' and so forth. The *Upamā-parivarta* says:"

"I pray that you will explain the causes and conditions for the sake of the fourfold assembly, so that they may be freed from doubt and regret"—this refers to those of middling capacity. The *Jùjì pǐn* (Chapter on Bestowing Prophecy) states:
"He constantly regrets and reflects upon the faults of the Hīnayāna, etc."—this also refers to those of middling capacity. The *Wǔbǎi dìzǐ pǐn* (Chapter on the Five Hundred Disciples) states:

"They prostrated at the Buddha’s feet, repenting their errors and reproaching themselves"—this refers to those of inferior capacity. Question: Regarding the three types of capacity who experience regret, there are both new and old instances of regret; which one [is being referred to]?
Is this so? The answer is that in the "Chapter on the Five Hundred Disciples," it says that remorse arises only upon hearing the prediction (*vyākaraṇa*);
this refers to new remorse. The others are old. Regarding the question of doubt, it applies generally to the three vehicles. Is the doubt of a bodhisattva also both new and old? Master Jizang says:
As for the old doubts of a bodhisattva, they arose from having previously received the teachings of the three vehicles; since they doubted the principles therein...

Third: one may doubt whether they will regress to the two lower stages, or one may doubt whether they will advance to attain the Buddha-way. As for the doubt now [expressed], it is a doubt regarding what the Buddha has taught: that the past and present are contradictory.

If there were three [vehicles] as previously stated, there should not have been a clarification here of the One; yet now, having distinguished the One, there should not have been a statement of three in the past.
Therefore, the "Expedient Means" chapter says: "When the Bodhisattvas hear this Dharma, the net of their doubts is entirely removed. Thus he asks the Bodhisattvas.
A new doubt arises: from what text does this emerge? Answer: In the *Śāriputraparipṛcchā*, it says: "The bodhisattvas who seek Buddhahood are, in great number, eighty thousand;
they desire to hear the complete path. One should know that bodhisattvas also have doubts. Question: Regarding these eighty thousand great beings...
"All are Dharma-body Bodhisattvas; how could there be room for doubt? Answer: "Śāriputra employs expedient means to guide and lead those who are truly capable.
Since Dharma-body Bodhisattvas should appear as if they were beginners, there is no fault. Question: "For what reason are doubts dispelled by teaching all three vehicles together?"

Regarding the listing of names for the bestowal of predictions (*vyākaraṇa*), there is no mention of *pratyekabuddhas* alone. The answer is that this does not obstruct their inclusion within the three vehicles;

however, because the faculties (*indriya*) of those with the *pratyekabuddha* disposition had not yet matured at the assembly of the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka*, they were not listed by name. Yet, even without being named, they receive the prediction.

This is because, while the removal of doubts and the seeking of the vehicle were discussed based on what was previously explained, their specific fruition was not mentioned. Thus, the subsequent statement, "All those who seek the three vehicles," refers back to what was said before. Alternatively, it may simply be...
This was spoken according to their specific capacities; it does not necessarily require that they have already directed themselves toward [the Mahāyāna] or severed their doubts.

Regarding the subsequent refutation of attachments in the commentary, there are three parts: first, identifying those who hold the attachments; second, the actual exposition on removing those attachments. The subsequent citations explain and establish [the meaning]. Regarding those who can grasp [this], within the first section on persons, there are two parts: first, the śrāvakas; second, the bodhisattvas. Within the section on śrāvakas, there are two further parts:
first, the enumeration of distinctions; second, the citation of treatises for explanation. Within the former, there are again two parts: first, a general enumeration.
The subsequent citation clarifies this.
The commentary states: "There are two types of śrāvakas... those of indeterminate nature. This is a general enumeration of the two kinds of śrāvakas.
Those whose roots of goodness are exhausted at the time of nirvāṇa are called śrāvakas of fixed nature; they are distinct from bodhisattvas and others, and are thus designated as such.
The remaining virtues within the body—namely liberation, supernormal powers (*abhijñā*), excellence, pervasiveness, and so forth—are collectively termed "wholesome roots" (*kuśalamūla*).

In the *Mahāyānasaṃparigraha-śāstra*, these are taken as that which is "suddenly abandoned" when what is to be abandoned is relinquished; they are like the extinction of a lamp’s flame, which does not abide in any direction, or [like] untainted seeds (*anāsravabīja*).
This is called "wholesome roots. One should examine this carefully.
Regarding the *Yogācārabhūmi-śāstra* and the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka-sūtra-upadeśa*, the text cited below clarifies the distinctions among the śrāvakas.

As for the commentary’s section from "the two types of overweening pride" to "arhat," it cites the latter here but places it at the beginning, similar to the treatment of the *Baozhi* (Kātyāyanīputra).

Those who have attained the first dhyāna as the first fruit and so forth are all persons of pride; their characteristics will be explained clearly below, so there is no need to list them here in advance.

Regarding the passage from "having already retreated three times" to "the spiritual lineage" (*gotra*): according to the *Yogācārabhūmi-śāstra*, this is called the "indeterminate lineage" (*aniyata-gotra*); according to the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka-sūtra-upadeśa*, it is... [text continues].
This is called "regression and re-awakening. Question: Why are they not the same? Answer: The *Commentary* states: "In the single assembly of the *Lotus Sūtra*, most [beings] have regressive minds;

it does not speak of the indeterminate nature (*aniyata-gotra*). The *Yogācārabhūmi-śāstra* speaks generally; it does not mention regressive minds. The indeterminate nature is broad in scope, whereas the term 'regressive mind' is narrow."
There is an indeterminate nature, because it is not a regressive mind.
Regarding the passage in the commentary stating that "sixty kalpas [pass] until [attaining] the small fruit," the text is cited below; one must examine and record it according to the verse. Question:
What kind of kalpa are these sixty kalpas? Answer: Although there is no definitive textual statement, by analogy with the meaning, they are not kalpas measured by days, months, or years.

Regarding the phrase "this kalpa": according to the principle of the relative duration of time, this should correspond to an *utkarṣa-kalpa* (increasing kalpa) or an *apakarṣa-kalpa* (decreasing kalpa).
As for the commentary’s statement, "it is not of indeterminate nature... because it is of indeterminate nature," this serves as a restrictive exclusion.

There are those of indeterminate nature who are termed "regressive minds" (*hāni-citta*); there are others of indeterminate nature who are merely termed "indeterminate" (*aniyata*) and are not termed "regressive minds. Therefore, it says, "it is not indeterminate."

[The] nature [of these]. All of these belong to the category of those subject to regression (*parihāṇa*). However, the meaning here is this: it is not the case that all those of indeterminate nature (*aniyata-gotra*) are exclusively of the category of regression;

there are some who are not subject to regression. Which ones are they? As the commentary (*śāstra*) states: "Furthermore, for instance, those who in the past had not yet sought the Great [Vehicle]," and so forth.
This refers to them.

Regarding the phrase "The *Sūtra Commentary on the Lotus Sutra* (*Fahua lun shu*) says": this refers to the subsequent citation of the commentary for explanation. Within this, there is first the citation and subsequently the explanation; that which begins from "those who have regressed from the bodhicitta" is it.

Regarding the passage "As for those who incline toward tranquility... causing them to resolve their minds": these are those with the overweening pride (*abhimāna*) of inclining toward tranquility, whom the Buddha does not grant a prediction (*vyākaraṇa*). Why? Because... [text continues].
Because their faculties were not yet mature, the Buddha did not grant them a prediction. As for the Bodhisattva Never-Disparaging, he granted predictions to these two individuals, as the sutra says:

"When you practice the bodhisattva path, you shall attain Buddhahood. According to the treatises, a bodhisattva grants a prediction in order to cause others to resolve their minds [for enlightenment];

it is not that they have actually attained Buddhahood at that moment. *She-lun* (the *Mahāyānasaṃgraha*) states: "There are two kinds of generating the mind: first, the generation of the mind of aspiration (*praṇidhāna-citta*)."

Regarding the "aspiration" (cittotpāda): there are two types of aspirational mind. The first is the superior [aspiration], which is the initial stage; the second is the inclination toward tranquility (*śamatha*). Taken together, these are collectively termed "arousing the mind" (*cittotpāda*).
Furthermore, there are two kinds of bodhisattvas: first, those who are beginners (*ādikarmika*); and second, those who have long practiced and reached the vessel of realization.

This concerns responding according to disposition and bestowing predictions [of enlightenment], as in the *Śrīmālā-sūtra*. A bodhisattva is capable of shouldering four great responsibilities: for those seeking bodhi, they bestow the Bodhisattva Vehicle and so forth;
for beginners who have not yet discerned their faculties, they simply cause them to make a general vow, thinking, "I shall become a Buddha.

This is precisely what the *Prajñāpāramitā-sūtra* means when it says, "I shall cause all to enter nirvana without remainder. The practice of *Adhimātra-gaurava* (Not Disparaging) is identical to this.

Regarding the statement in the *Śāstra* that "the Bodhisattva is endowed with the causal nature for receiving the prediction," the *Cè* (攝) says: Question: According to the *Yogācārabhūmi-śāstra*, one is said to be "endowed with the causes" only when both the rational nature (*li-xing*) and the causal nature (*yin-xing*) are present.
Now, since there is only the rational nature here, how can it be called "endowed"? Answer: This sutra and treatise state that they manifest to sentient beings that all possess Buddha-nature.
If this were not the rational nature, how could all beings possess it? The Master of the *Śāstra* relies on this and speaks in terms of the rational nature.

"Endowment" (*yoga*) means "complete. It refers to that which all sentient beings equally possess; therefore, the name "endowment" is established. There are further explanations, which will be fully detailed below. Question:

Even when a Bodhisattva grants a prediction (*vyākaraṇa*), it still causes faith to arise. Why, then, does the Buddha abandon [this teaching]? Answer: The Buddha’s prediction concerns the attainment of Buddhahood.

Necessarily, there must be such matters as the name of the land and so forth; however, for those with overweening pride (*adhimāna*), who have not yet planted roots of goodness, these matters do not exist, and therefore the Buddha did not bestow a prediction upon them.

Furthermore, another explanation states: just as during the time of Buddha King of Majestic Sound (*Vaiśvānara-rāja*), those whose faculties were not yet mature were not predicted by that Buddha, but later, in the age of the Dharma’s decay (*mappō*), the Bodhisattva Never-Disparaging bestowed predictions upon them—what harm is there in this being the case for those whose faculties were not yet mature during the lifetime of Śākyamuni?

The Buddha did not grant a prediction. Later, during the final dharma age, there was someone who granted a prediction; it was not necessarily Śākyamuni himself, but rather he deferred to his disciples, instructing them to deliver the prediction.
Because the three periods of time are identical, he cited this as an example.

Regarding the passage in the commentary stating, "Those who have entered *śama* (quiescence) lack the nature of greatness," the following explains the general meaning of the Master of the Commentary (*Sūzhǔ*) concerning the main treatise (*lùwén*).
The treatise states: "Because the roots of the *śrāvakas* who have entered *śama* are not yet mature, the Buddha does not grant them a prediction (*vyākaraṇa*), whereas the Bodhisattvas do.

The Master of the Commentary’s intent is as follows: The treatise says that for those who have entered *śama*, their roots are "not yet mature" (*máishú*). This should rather be stated as "unripe" (*bùshú*). If [the roots] were superior...
Your statement that there is no error is not quite right. As for those who have entered into tranquility (*śama*), they originally lack the Mahāyāna nature;

how, then, can one discuss whether they are mature or immature? In principle, it should be said: "Those who have entered into tranquility lack the Mahāyāna nature; the Buddha did not grant them a prediction [of enlightenment].

As for the Bodhisattvas granting a prediction, this is based on their possessing the causal conditions for the principle, and because they possess the capacity to cause others to have faith and not be deluded regarding the Mahāyāna; thus they grant the prediction. It is not otherwise.

Regarding those who have entered the state of tranquility (*śamaikāyana*), because their faculties (*indriya*) are not yet matured, they shall become matured later. The Bodhisattva speaks to them and grants them a prediction (*vyākaraṇa*).

Furthermore, this does not mean that he causes them to generate the mind set on the Mahāyāna by saying, "You shall become Buddhas," while granting a prediction to those who have entered the state of tranquility. If that were so—
"Why is it unnecessary to grant a prediction? The commentary immediately following states: "The Bodhisattva’s vow-mind employs skillful means to transform them, causing them to give rise to faith;
for this reason, no prediction is granted. How is this known to be so? The text subsequently cites passages from the *Prajñāpāramitā Sūtra* as proof, which can be fully understood therein.
The remainder of the text may be understood.

Regarding the phrase "the Bodhisattvas are also twofold" in the commentary: this clarifies the Bodhisattvas below. The word "for now" (*qie*) is used because two types were previously listed for the Śrāvakas;
since these Bodhisattvas likewise have two types, the word "for now" is employed.

Regarding the commentary’s statement, "Because the number of births is few, or because they are made non-existent," the *Śāstra* (the *Abhidharmakośabhāṣya*) explains: those who have attained the first three fruits possess seven births and so forth, which is called "few in number of births.

Those who have attained the fruit of no-more-learning (*aśaikṣa*) have exhausted their births, which is termed "making them non-existent. Alternatively, while still in the stage of an ordinary person (*pṛthagjana*), they pass through sixty kalpas.
Regarding the cultivation over three lifetimes: within this current life, from birth until its end, it is provisionally termed "non-existent";

or, in the case of one who has attained the first fruit (*srotāpanna*) and is able to leap over to attain the fruit [of arhatship], it is likewise called "entirely non-existent. Some say that the *Nirvāṇa Sūtra* speaks of two types of faculties:

the first is those of sharp faculty (*tīkṣṇendriya*), who are able to leap over to attain the fruit, attaining the fruit of arhatship in this very body, which is also termed "entirely non-existent. The second...

This refers to those of dull faculties who attain the fruits [of the path] sequentially. The *Śāstra* (the *Abhidharmakośabhāṣya*) states: Question: Regarding the meaning of "sudden" and "gradual," does it depend on the number of births? If it does not, why is it necessary to mention it? Answer:

The purpose of citing the number of births and so forth is to demonstrate the attainment of the state of an Ārya. Once the state of an Ārya is attained, there is a distinction between those still in training (*śaikṣa*) and those beyond training (*aśaikṣa*).

This demonstrates the difference between these two types, both of whom are capable of turning back toward higher progress; it is not intended to prove the doctrine of gradual enlightenment by means of the number of births. Question:

Although the principle may be understood, the mention of "numerous births" (jātis) is not essential. Furthermore, by speaking of the two vehicles (dviyāna), one already encompasses everything; so why rely on the enumeration of births?

Answer: If the number were not mentioned, it might be feared that one could not fully comprehend those who are both with and without training (śaikṣa-aśaikṣa), as all of them are capable of turning toward [the Mahāyāna].
Therefore, it is not without necessity.

Regarding the commentary on "the two types of ordinary beings," the *She* (攝) states: "The ordinary stages of the two vehicles possess the two types of lineage (*gotra*) and cultivate the practices of the two vehicles;
until they have attained the two fruits, all [stages] up to this point are collectively termed the 'two types of ordinary beings.'"

Regarding the statement, "One who has previously given rise to two minds and previously cultivated two practices," this refers to having given rise to the mind of the Two Vehicles and having previously cultivated the practices of the Two Vehicles.

As for the phrase, "Because the commentary possesses that nature and because one cultivates those practices," the former clause clarifies that one has previously given rise to the two minds mentioned above,
while the latter clause clarifies that one has previously cultivated the two practices mentioned above.
The commentary states: "From 'hearing, contemplating, and awakening through understanding' up to 'why must there be realization'? This passage addresses an objection. The objection asks:

"If one has already generated the two types of resolve and so forth, this is called gradual awakening; yet since one has not realized the fruit, how can it be called awakening? Therefore, the commentary responds:
"Awakening through hearing, contemplating, and understanding is provisionally termed 'awakening. Why must one realize the fruit to be called subsequent awakening?"
Regarding the commentary’s statement from “Furthermore, moreover” up to “parts, etc.,” first the meaning is explained, and subsequently the text is interpreted.

The *Mahāyānasaṃgrahābhidharmasamuccaya-śāstra*, chapter thirteen, states: “The person who has not yet accumulated the provisions; the person who has both accumulated and not yet accumulated the provisions;
and the person who has already accumulated the provisions. Thus it speaks of these three types of persons.

Because the factors conducive to liberation (*mokṣabhāgīya*), the factors conducive to liberation, and the factors conducive to penetration (*nirvedhabhāgīya*) each consist of three grades, [the definition] is given in relation to that which can induce the factors conducive to penetration and the clear observation of the truths (*satyābhisamaya*).

Accordingly, the characteristic of pure faith and resolute conviction (*adhimukti*) regarding the truths—whether indeterminate or determinate at the very moment of arising—is the factor conducive to liberation. That is to say, in...

This dharma, characterized by the patient acceptance of the thorough investigation of dharmas (*dharmavicaya-kṣānti*), constitutes the aids to penetration (*nirvedhabhāgīya*). These follow their respective order because faith is predominant and wisdom is predominant.
Among these, the three grades of the aids to penetration refer to those excluding the Supreme Mundane Dharmas (*laukikāgradharma*).

This is because the nature of the Supreme Mundane Dharmas consists of only a single moment and necessarily does not continue; at the very moment they arise, one definitely enters the Path of Seeing (*darśanamārga*).

Regarding the observation: because it is not the preceding stage, the text decisively states that within the stages of the *sambhāra* (provisioning) and *prayoga* (preparatory application), there are each three grades.
According to their sequence, these correspond to the times when [the path] is not yet determined and when it is already determined, occurring in this very life.

However, the *prayoga* stage is divided into three grades—those not yet determined and those already determined—which occur in this very life during the stages of *uṣmagata*, *mūrdhan*, and *kṣānti*, excluding the *laukikāgradharma*.
The first dharma lasts for only a single moment; it is called "non-continuous" and is indivisible.

Nevertheless, when it is said that at the very moment this [dharma] arises, one necessarily enters into clear realization (*abhisamaya*), this is stated in reference to its arising at that specific moment. As for the previously mentioned "aids to liberation" (*mokṣabhāgīya*), the statement that they arise at that very moment [refers to their initial production].

This is explained in terms of a single lifetime (*ekajātīya*). Another interpretation holds that both [the preceding and following statements] are likewise explained in terms of a single lifetime; for it is said that the "Supreme Mundane Dharma" (*laukikāgradharma*) occurs at this very moment of birth.

Since the Supreme Mundane Dharma is excluded [from the category of the "Patience"], it is clear that [the discussion] refers to a single lifetime. Although the "Superior Patience" (*adhimātrākṣānti*) lasts for only a single moment (*kṣaṇa*), it is nonetheless subsumed within this framework of a single lifetime.
It is still separated from the Supreme Mundane Dharma (*laukikāgradharma*), for one does not enter the Path of Seeing (*darśanamārga*) immediately in the very next moment after its arising.

Furthermore, it is divided into three stages—mild (*mṛdu*), peak (*mūrdhan*), and patience (*kṣānti*)—because there are three periods. That treatise further enumerates six types of factors conducive to penetration (*nirvedhabhāgīya*):

first, those conducive to penetration; second, superior progress (*viśeṣagamana*); third, thorough comprehension (*prativedha*); fourth, further transformation (*anyathābhāva*); fifth, the single birth (*ekajāti*); and sixth, the final [birth].
Seated, one initially gives rise to [a state] that takes the objects of the truths as its cognitive domain. This inferior grade of wholesome root then transforms into a middle grade;

this is called the "superior advancement" (viśeṣabhāgīya) stage of the aids to penetration (*nirvedhabhāgīya*). Because it is superior compared to the preceding inferior grade, this wholesome root increases further until it reaches the superior grade.
Within this very life, one becomes definitively capable of penetrating the principles of the truths; this is called "penetration" (*prativedha*).

[He] attains [realization]. Furthermore, within this stage, those of indeterminate lineage who turn toward supreme enlightenment or toward the state of a pratyekabuddha, seeking the teacherless, self-realized enlightenment, and thus transition to another birth, are said to be "those who have turned elsewhere.

If one is certain to attain realization in this very life, they are said to be "one-life [attainers]. If one is certain to attain realization in this very session, they are said to be "one-[session] attainers."

[This refers to] the stages conducive to penetration (*nirvedhabhāgīya*) within a single sitting. However, in the present text, it simply states "already determined for birth" (*niyata-utpatti*), which refers to the moment of birth itself and the stages conducive to penetration within a single sitting.
This is intended to include those with fewer births; therefore, other cases are not mentioned. The summary of this intent is as follows:

this is based on the stage of an ordinary person (*pṛthagjana*) looking toward the path of seeing (*darśanamārga*) to describe the number [of births]. Question: Since the explanation regarding awakening is based upon hearing and reflection (*śruta-cintā*), how can it be applied here?

Why are "births" (*janman*) and so forth cited as logical proofs? Answer: One who has merely once given rise to the two minds and once practiced the two paths is called one of gradual enlightenment (*anupūrva-abhisambodha*).

How much more so for those who have already departed [from the stage of ordinary beings] and whose number of births until reaching the path of vision (*darśana-mārga*) is few; such persons are not called those of gradual enlightenment.

The term "number of births" is intended to prove that through textual study and cultivation, one is also called one of gradual enlightenment; it does not mean that one must first prove entry into the path of vision by means of the number of births before practicing.

This is a great practice; however, it was not the original intention of that Master. There are two explanations in the commentary (*śāstra*). Regarding the interpretation based on the number of births, this is not the intention of the commentator.
When the Master of the Commentary formerly expounded upon the section concerning the number of births, various virtuous teachers disputed the meaning of these sudden and gradual [attainments].

Because some people used this number of births as a criterion for judgment, [the author] merely records it here. The Master of the Commentary simply relies on the fact that one may either attain the two types of sages or practice...
Regarding the two types of practice: those who turn toward the Great [Vehicle] are termed "gradual enlighteners.

The commentary on the sutra, based on the determination of kalpas, refers to the passage from the *Nirvāṇa Sūtra* in this assembly. If it is said that they have not yet entered the stage of the noble ones (*ārya*).
However, those who possess the mind of dedication (*pariṇāmanā-citta*) are called "gradual awakeners" (*anupūrva-bodhaka*).

Why, then, does the *Nirvāṇa Sūtra* state that for a *srotāpanna*, the number of kalpas until the turning of the mind is eighty thousand kalpas and so forth, yet does not mention this for ordinary beings (*pṛthagjana*)? Therefore, the intent of the present assembly [of the sūtra] is evident.

The commentary [states]: "From 'What is taught in this sutra' up to 'does not deviate from the truth,' this excludes those who hold to the Middle Way. First, it describes the Śrāvakas; subsequently, it narrates the Bodhisattvas. Regarding the passage "What is taught in this sutra...
is for the purpose of transforming and bestowing predictions," this describes the Śrāvakas. However, the intended meaning is as follows:

according to the four types of Śrāvakas in the treatises, although the middle category is divided into two, when the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka-sūtra* was preached at a single assembly, it was primarily for those whose resolve had regressed, while also [addressing] others.

It is for the sake of transformation; because Pūrṇamaitrāyaṇīputra was present in the assembly, the meaning encompasses three [categories]. Regarding the "encompassing of the three" within the ten meanings of the *Mahāyānasaṃgraha*, there is no fixed lineage (*niyata-gotra*).
What is now called "the meaning encompasses" is the intended sense of the Commentary (the *Śāstra*). This means that the meaning encompasses those of fixed nature (*niyata-gotra*).
As for the "ten meanings," they shall be fully analyzed when we reach the chapter on the One Vehicle (*ekayāna*).
"Although it may also be for the two types of bodhisattvas (up to) 'there is no error,' this passage describes the intention of the bodhisattvas:

although this sūtra contains both sudden and gradual teachings, its main body (*śarīra*) is intended solely for those of gradual enlightenment; that is, it is for the benefit of the three grades of *śrāvakas* and others.
If one relies on the later part of the sūtra which says, 'When the bodhisattvas hear this Dharma, the net of their doubts is entirely removed,' then according to this meaning..."
Furthermore, as for the principle of sudden enlightenment, it remains unimpaired.

Regarding the statement in the *Commentary on the Mahāyānasaṃparigraha-śāstra* that "the ten meanings subsume the One Vehicle," the subsequent citation from the section on "Establishing [the Meaning]" is divided into two parts:

first, up to the phrase "the intent of adhering to the Small Vehicle," which clarifies the adherence to the Small Vehicle; second, from the phrase "that is, the *Mahāyānasaṃparigraha-śāstra* says" onwards, which cites and establishes the argument.
The commentary explains the three ways of refining the mind: first, when discouraged by the vastness of bodhicitta, one refines it by comparing others to oneself;

second, when discouraged by the difficulty of practicing the myriad deeds, one refines it by reflecting on oneself and increasing one's cultivation; third, when discouraged by the difficulty of realizing the transformation of the basis (*āśraya-parāvṛtti*), one refines it by comparing the coarse to the sublime.
However, both Vasubandhu’s *Mahāyānasaṃgrahabhāṣya* and [Asaṅga’s] *Mahāyānasaṃgraha* extensively clarify these characteristics. For now, I shall provide an exposition based on Vasubandhu’s work.
Its sixth fascicle states: The treatise says: "In immeasurable world-systems, immeasurable persons and sentient beings realize unexcelled, perfect, and complete enlightenment moment by moment.
This is the first way of training the mind. Based on this intent...
Joy. One is able to practice the perfections such as generosity.
Having already attained such an intention, by means of this, one will fulfill the cultivation of the perfections such as generosity with little effort;
this is called the second training of the mind. If one possesses wholesome qualities that are subject to obstacles, at the time of death, they may immediately...
"I love all my own bodies; they are born complete. I possess excellent qualities and unimpeded virtues.
Why, then, should I not attain all perfections at this time? This is called the third refinement of the mind. He himself explains:
"In this context, because one counteracts three types of despondency, one practices only these three refinements of the mind. Such is the reason.

Why is this? Because when bodhisattvas hear that unsurpassed, perfectly complete enlightenment is most supreme, profoundly deep, vast, and difficult to realize, their minds may become discouraged and retreat.
To counteract this, they cultivate the first refinement of the mind.
Furthermore, when bodhisattvas hear that the perfections (*pāramitās*) to be practiced are most supreme, profoundly deep, vast, and difficult to realize, their minds...
Consequently, one becomes discouraged. To counteract this, one cultivates the second refinement of the mind.

Regarding the statement that "by means of this aspiration (*āśaya*), one is able to practice the perfections (*pāramitā*) such as generosity," the term "aspiration" here refers to faith (*śraddhā*) and zeal (*chanda*).

It means that the Bodhisattva develops a profound conviction and understanding regarding the perfections as having true existence, possessing virtuous qualities, and being capable of accomplishment. This is called...
This constitutes faith. Having attained deep faith and understanding, one takes delight in the desire to practice; this is called aspiration (*chanda*).

Once a bodhisattva has attained such faith and aspiration, through their natural inclination (*āśaya*), they will, with little exertion of effort, cultivate the six perfections (*ṣaṭ-pāramitā*) and bring them to fulfillment.
Furthermore, these bodhisattvas possess skillfulness in reflecting upon and discerning the Buddha’s profound and vast teachings.
At the time of turning [the mind], one reflects thus: "Such unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment is difficult to realize;
it can only be realized by crossing over a single moment of thought. Thereupon, the mind becomes discouraged. To counteract this, one cultivates the third refinement of the mind.
"I possess that which is wondrously excellent. Within all ten stages (*bhūmi*), I have accumulated the wondrously excellent provisions of merit and wisdom.

That which is unobstructed and excellent refers to the diamond-like concentration (*vajropama-samādhi*), which can shatter the subtle, extremely difficult-to-break obstructions consisting of the heavy residues (*dauṣṭhulya*) residing within the bones.
Immediately following this concentration, one attains the fundamental transformation (*āśrayaparivṛtti*) through liberation from all obstructions. Why, at such a time, would it not be so?

Regarding "attaining all perfections," the intended meaning here is as follows: with respect to liberation from obstacles, at the time similar to that of death, the knowledge of all modes (*sarvākārajñatā*) is perfected in its essence, just as it was previously.
Furthermore, in this context, there are three ways of tempering the mind:

namely, that the bodhisattvas possess no deficiency in their roots of virtue (*kuśalamūla*), and are sustained by the power of those roots; by means of this power, they are then able to perform the threefold tempering.
One grinds the mind; the mind does not retreat or become disheartened. First, one should demonstrate the first stage of grinding the mind:
that within the human realm, across immeasurable worlds and immeasurable sentient beings, one is able to realize unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment at every single moment.
"Why is it that I alone am unable to realize [this] now? Next, the second kind of mental fortitude (*cittaparidamanā*) shall be demonstrated.

It refers to when bodhisattvas reflect as follows: "Since this intention of mine is free from all obstacles—because there are no obstacles such as stinginess regarding the *pāramitās*—the *pāramitās* shall become perfected without effort; therefore, I shall realize Buddhahood."
Regarding *bodhi*, the third refinement of the mind will be explained hereafter.

As for those whose goodness is obstructed—meaning they achieve that goodness through worldly means—even such obstructed goodness results in the birth of a fully perfected and desirable physical existence at the time of death;
how much more so, then, for me, who have achieved goodness through unobstructed goodness? Should I not thereby attain Buddhahood?
"Unsurpassed enlightenment—this is impossible. The treatise says: There is a verse on this point: "The sentient beings in the human realm are infinite in number;
since they can realize equal enlightenment in every moment of thought, one should not be discouraged. Those with pure mental dispositions are able to practice generosity and the like;
these superior ones have already attained [the capacity], and thus they can cultivate generosity and so forth. When such virtuous ones face death, they attain..."
One’s own fulfillment is achieved according to one’s will; since supreme goodness arises from eternal abandonment, how could it not be perfected? Furthermore, another verse elsewhere says:
"If all sentient beings in the worlds of the ten directions can swiftly realize the fruit of the Sugata in every thought-moment, and they are already great men, so am I;
I should not disparage myself or succumb to despondency. This is the foremost [encouragement]. You have already wandered through the evil realms for many eons; [therefore...]

"If one can still transcend even while undergoing increasing suffering, then by cultivating a small amount of merit now, one shall attain Bodhi; thus, one should not give rise to despondency regarding this great benefit.
This is the second. "An ordinary person on the stage of thinness (tanubhūmi) first resolves their mind and aims for the distant realization of the fruit of Bodhi;
I have already exerted diligence through many kalpas, and should not regress or sink into the cycle of saṃsāra. This is the third. These are the three kinds of refinement.

The self-explanation of the treatise is clear in its textual structure; there is no need for further prolixity. As for the remaining analysis, we shall follow the *She-shi* (Commentary on the Compendium). It says: Question:

Based on the three types of refinement (*parikarma*), one has not yet ascended to the stage of a noble one (*ārya*). How can it be said that "I possess wondrous goodness" and "unobstructed goodness"? Answer: This is discussed from the perspective of what is destined to occur.
If one practices without ceasing, one will certainly attain these two kinds of goodness. Since these two kinds of goodness exist [in the future], [one may speak thus].

One may not yet obtain the fruit, but having already obtained it at an improper time, this is called "possessing wondrous goodness. Question: In what stages or positions do these three refinements (*pariśodhana*) reside? Answer: There are two explanations.

First, it is said that they reside collectively in the initial stage of the ten levels of faith (*daśa-śraddhā*). Second, it is said that the first resides prior to the ten levels of faith and within the second [level] of the ten levels of faith;
the second resides prior to those ten levels of understanding (*daśa-vijñapti*) and within the position of the ten levels of understanding; and the third resides in that [position].
Because this occurs prior to the ten dedications and during the stage of dedication (*pariṇāmanā*), the *Vijñaptimātratāsiddhi* states:

"In this stage of the equipment (*sambhāra-avasthā*), although the two types of obstacles have not yet been suppressed or eliminated, when one cultivates the sublime practices, even if there are three kinds of despondency, one is able to exercise and temper the mind through three matters."
Regarding what is realized and cultivated, one is courageous and does not retreat. Furthermore, it is said that within the three stages, all three types of despondency apply;

there is no need for a specific correspondence. Question: Regarding the three kinds of refinement (*parikarma*), which dharma serves as the intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*) of each, both in terms of the subject that refines and the object that is refined?

Answer: The subject that refines generally takes the two wisdoms of hearing (*śruta*) and reflection (*cintā*) as its essence. This is because, through hearing, one generates the resolve and practices according to others.
By citing examples from others to stimulate one’s own mind, one comes to know through inference; therefore, this constitutes hearing and reflection (*śruta-cintā*).
As for the essence of what is cultivated, it consists of the innate lineage (*gotra*), the bodhicitta, and the four factors conducive to enlightenment (*bodhipakṣa-dharma*) and so forth.

That which is to be remedied is the three types of despondency, which are subsumed under the cognitive obscurations (*jñeyāvaraṇa*); these constitute its essence. Due to horizontal deliberation, one thinks, "I am incapable," and so forth.

The bodhisattva-mind is not the cause of the various practices; rather, because its fruit is difficult to attain, it is subsumed under the cognitive obscuration (*jñeyāvaraṇa*) of attachment to phenomena (*dharmagrāha*).
Question: What is the meaning of "refining" (*pariśodhana*)? Answer: It means to stimulate the mind so that it becomes sharp and intense, thereby counteracting despondency and withdrawal.
This is the meaning of refining. Furthermore, it is like refining gold and is similar to polishing a mirror; it causes the mind to become pure, and thus the name "refining" is established.

Regarding the commentary’s statement, “Severing the obstacles of the four bases... as for discrimination”: that which takes the dharma and its meaning as its object, the *Subcommentary* (*Chao*) explains:

"Dharma" refers to the words that express; "meaning" refers to the significance expressed. The sixth fascicle of Vasubandhu’s *Mahāyānasaṃgraha-bhāṣya* states: "That which resembles words and resembles meanings."

The *Śāstra* (Commentary) states: "While it appears externally extensive, in reality it exists only internally. According to this, that which exists resembles non-existence; the internal resembles the external.

Regarding the "four locations," the sixth fascicle of Vasubandhu’s *Mahāyānasaṃgraha-bhāṣya* states: "Because of being free from the mental orientations (*manasikāra*) of Śrāvakas and Pratyekabuddhas.
The commentary explains: "This means because one has severed all mental orientations such as those of the Śrāvakas. The *Saṃgraha* (Summary) states: "'By' means 'due to.'"

Regarding "meaning" (*artha*): because one is free from the obstacle of mental attention (*manasikāra*), one is able to enter the characteristics of the knowable (*jñeyalakṣaṇa*). The remaining three [stages] are to be understood accordingly.

As for the phrase "because of abandoning mental attention," this explains what it means to be "free from mental attention"; it indicates the cause [of that freedom]. This term "abandoning" (*prahāṇa*) refers merely to suppression (*vibhava*). This applies to the latter three stages for now.
