Matters such as these arts and so forth; because one obtains food through them, they are called "mouth-maintenance" (*mukha-bhāṇḍa*). When minor arts are improper, they are termed "mouth-maintenance.
Thus, the three types of action (*trikarma*) incited by greed and hatred are called "wrong livelihood" (*mithyājīva*). As a verse says: "Worldly wrong views are difficult to eliminate."
Because they constantly hold divergent views, they are "heretics" (*tīrthika*); because their lives are in peril [due to such views], they are "teachers" (*śāstṛ*).
Because their requisites belong to others, these five names—from the initial going forth (*pravrajyā*)—should be understood as being cultivated gradually until one reaches the status of a teacher.

The *Saṃgraha* says: Question: The name "bhikṣu" contains the meaning of "begging. Should all other beggars also be called bhikṣus? Answer: The name "bhikṣu" possesses [the specific qualities of]... [text fragment ends].
Regarding these five meanings, others who do not possess all five are not called bhikṣus.
As for the statement that "the union of principle and phenomenon (li-shi) results in the various names [of the Saṃgha]," this means:

when they equally realize the one True Principle, it is called "harmony of principle" (*li-he*), as it accords with the pure characteristics of the scriptures. When they share the same precepts, views, and livelihoods without contradiction, it is called "harmony of phenomenon" (*shi-he*).
Regarding the statement that those numbering three or more receive the name "Saṃgha," the *Fayuan* states: In Sanskrit it is called *saṃgha*, which here means "assembly.

However, those numbering three or more all possess the essential nature of the Saṃgha; this is because the term follows the sense of plurality. According to the law of that country (India), even a single individual is termed a "name" (*nāman*).
Two constitute a body; from three upwards, they are called "many. As in the performance of formal monastic acts (*karmavācanā*), four persons are required for it to be accomplished.

One person makes the announcement (*jñapti*), saying: "Venerable Saṃgha, listen. Since the other three persons in harmony are designated as the "Saṃgha," if these four together were the Saṃgha, how could the one who makes the announcement be part of that very Saṃgha while announcing it himself?
This is to manifest the harmony derived from a plurality of persons; thus, from three upwards, all are permitted [to perform such acts].
Regarding "famous monks" (*nāma-bhikṣu*): if they are monks who perform administrative affairs, they consist of four, five, ten, twenty, or more persons.

Regarding the six phrases in the commentary (up to the word) "ultimate" (*niṣṭhā-gata*): this is the first part of the subsequent praise of virtues, which first lists them and subsequently explains them.
As for the "newly translated and old treatises," *Cai* says: the *Prajñāpāramitā* sūtras and others translated by the Tripiṭaka Master of the Tang dynasty are called...
Regarding the "New Sūtra": the earlier translations of this sūtra are termed "Old. Furthermore, when referring to the "New Sūtra," it is actually other ancient sūtras;

as for the statement that there are sixteen, this refers to the fact that the *Vyākhyāyukti* (Treatise on the Explanation) comments upon these sūtras. Question: Why do the numbers of the sūtras and the treatises differ? Answer:

It is said that the assembly of the constant retinue never fails to gather, and they praise [the Buddha's virtues] everywhere. Therefore, Kumārajīva briefly praised his virtues, while Maitreya (Devagupta) intended to demonstrate the interpretation of a single sūtra.
Praising the virtues (guṇa-stava): This is intended to cause others to recognize the multitude of virtues; it is for this purpose that the praise of virtues is explained in detail. Question:

Why do the praises of virtues in various sūtras differ in length—some being more extensive and others more concise? Answer: There are two explanations. First, the translators varied between providing detailed accounts and abbreviated ones.
Second, those who compiled the Dharma praised the virtues to greater or lesser extents, as these praises were all placed there by the compilers (saṃgītikāra).

Regarding the three interpretations in the *Śāstra*, in the subsequent explanation, one first relies on the *Śāstra* for its exposition and subsequently provides a general critical analysis (*paryeṣaṇā*).
Within these three sections, each first relies on the *Śāstra* and subsequently explains the scriptural text (*sūtra*). "Seeking" (*mīmāṃsā*) means to rest.
Regarding the phrase "the sequence of ascending excellence" (shang-shang qi), it refers to cases where the lower [explanation] clarifies the upper, or the upper clarifies the lower;
these are collectively termed "ascending excellence. For example, the second point—that all outflows (*āsrava*) have been exhausted—explains the first term, *arhat*.
In the first phrase, "Arhat" is that which is produced; thus it is called "arising above. This is what is meant by "arising above" being designated as "above.
In the second phrase, "all outflows are exhausted" is that which produces; this is called the "arising of that which arises above. Therefore, it is termed "arising above.

There are many such categories like these, which are termed "arising above-above. The following explains the above in this manner. If one were to explain the below by means of the above, for instance:

Just as the second phrase, "all outflows are exhausted," explains the third [phrase], "no further afflictions remain"—wherein the former phrase is the "ariser" (the cause), termed an "upper ariser" (*ūrdhvotpāda*), meaning that the act of arising is designated as "upper";

and the latter phrase is the "arisen" (the effect), termed simply "arising" (*utpāda*), which is situated above that [act of arising]—since there are many such analogies, it is called "upper-upper arising" (*ūrdhvordhvotpāda*). However, according to the sub-commentary (*ṭīkā*):

The self-explanation: Now, for the sake of the initial overview, the *shu* (sub-commentary) refers to the words of the treatise (*lun*) [extending] to the term "Arhat. This citation of the text serves as an explanation; it refers to treatises such as the *Vijñaptimātratāsiddhi*.

This refers to the *Vijñaptimātratāsiddhi*. There are three meanings for the term "arhat" (*arhan*). The present statement, "one who has eternally destroyed the thieves of the afflictions," constitutes one meaning.
To cite this intent is to establish the preceding point that the "Teacher alone" (the Buddha) is an Arhat because he has eliminated all currently active outflows (*āsrava*).

Śèpò (攝) says: Question: For those beyond training (*aśaikṣa*), both the seeds and the manifest [afflictions] are exhausted. Why is it not stated that they are both [Arhats] by means of the second and third [meanings]?
[This concludes] the first section. Question: Why is it so? Answer: Bodhisattvas of the eighth stage and above who have attained sudden enlightenment are also called *arhats*.

However, they only truly deserve that name when their seeds of reality are exhausted; thus, those at the eighth stage are not included among the [ordinary] *arhats*. Here, in order to show that the term applies generally to them as well, "exhaustion of outflows" (*āsravakṣaya*) is used to explain the *arhat*.
Based on this, I shall briefly clarify the differences in the Sanskrit names. Now, there are three names for an *arhat*: the first is...
The first is named Aruḥ; the second, Arhat; and the third, Araha. These correspond respectively to "slayer of thieves," "worthy of offerings," and "non-arising.
If explained in relation to the causal stage, the cause is called "terrifying Māra," while upon reaching the fruit, it is termed "slayer of thieves."
In the causal stage, one is called a "beggar" (bhikṣu); upon reaching the fruit, one is called "worthy of offerings" (arhat). In the causal stage, one is called "one who destroys evil";
in the fruit stage, one is called "non-arising. Now, these three names—such as "slayer of thieves"—are all designations used for the fruit stage.

Regarding the commentary’s statement that “the active manifestation (*samudācāra*) of afflictions is called an outflow (*āsrava*”), this explains the etymology of the term *āsrava*. Furthermore, the first chapter of the *Abhidharmasamuccaya* states:

“Because it causes the mind to flow continuously and scatter without interruption, it is called an outflow. What does this mean? It refers to flowing out through the external gates; thus, the outflow of ignorance (*avidyā-āsrava*) is established.
This meaning of causing the mind to flow continuously and scatter without interruption differs from the [other] meanings of the term *āsrava*. If...

The *Abhidharmakośa* states: "They detain sentient beings, causing them to dwell long in saṃsāra, or causing them to circulate within saṃsāra from the Peak of Existence (*bhavāgra*) down to the Avīci Hell.
Because they flow forth incessantly through the six wound-gates (*ṣaḍ-vraṇamukha*) via that continuity (*saṃtati*), they are called 'outflows' (*āsrava*).
According to Vasubandhu’s exposition of the Sautrāntika school: "If one explains it correctly, they flow toward all objects..."
The commentary states: "A continuous succession; because outflows (āsrava) leak forth without ceasing, they are called 'leaks' (*asrava*).
The sub-commentary (*śūtra*) explains from "the path of seeing (*darśanamārga*) of the desire realm" up to "desire-leak" (*kāma-āsrava*). This identifies the essential nature of the desire-leak.

Regarding the "forty [afflictions] of the path of seeing in the desire realm," this refers to the analytical afflictions (*vibhava-kleśa*) of the desire realm that arise in delusion regarding the Four Noble Truths. Since there are ten [afflictions] for each truth, they total forty.

40. Question: For what reason is it thus? Answer: Indeed, there is both a general and a specific confusion regarding the characteristics of the Truths (*satya*). The general refers to ten types, all of which are confused about the Four Truths. Why is this so?
Because Suffering (*duḥkha*) and its Origin (*samudaya*) are the causes and bases for that [confusion], while Cessation (*nirodha*) and the Path (*mārga*) are the objects of fear for it.
Regarding the phrase "causes and bases": first, there is the cause; second, there is the basis. Thus, the *Abhidharma-śāstra* states: [text follows].
It is said: The two truths of suffering and its origin are both of one kind—namely, the causes and conditions of affliction—and they also serve as their basis.

Therefore, by being deluded regarding these causes, conditions, and bases, one gives rise to various wrong practices; one speaks of cessation and the path as places of fear, and by nature does not accord with them.
These ten increase only by giving rise to confusion, hesitation, and so forth. Thus, the Abhidharma-śāstra states:

"By the power of the afflictions (*kleśa*), one takes pleasure in *saṃsāra* and conceives of the pure dharmas as being like a precipice. Furthermore, various non-Buddhists falsely give rise to all manner of inverted conceptualizations regarding the truths of Cessation and the Path.
Therefore, these ten doubts are all confused regarding Cessation and the Path, giving rise to various wrong views.

The [ten] courses of action and the various afflictions (*kleśa*) both arise from two conditions. If one considers their specific delusions, the two [views of self and extremes] are deluded only regarding suffering (*duḥkha*), while the eight [remaining afflictions] are deluded regarding all four truths.

The view of a self-body (*satkāyadṛṣṭi*) arises only with respect to the locus of the fruit. However, taking the general delusion into account, all ten afflictions are deluded regarding the four truths.

As for the statement "along with the twenty secondary afflictions (*upakleśa*) such as anger (*krodha*) and resentment (*upanāha*)," the verse of the *Vijñaptimātratāsiddhi-śāstra* says: "The secondary afflictions are..."

Anger, enmity, concealment, vexation, envy, parsimony, deceit, guile, harmfulness, pride, lack of shame, lack of dread, restlessness, torpor, lack of faith, laziness, heedlessness, forgetfulness, distraction, and lack of clear comprehension.
Question: Why are these twenty called secondary afflictions (*upakleśa*)? Answer:
Because they are specific states (*avasthā-viśeṣa*) of the primary afflictions and are of the nature of their outflow (*niṣyanda*), they are called secondary afflictions.

Regarding the afflictions (*kleśa*): the ten [mental factors] beginning with anger (*krodha*), as well as forgetfulness (*muṣitasmṛti*), lack of clear comprehension (*asaṃprajanya*), and heedlessness (*pramāda*), are designated as derivative afflictions (*upakleśa*) because they are specific states or modalities of the aforementioned primary afflictions such as greed (*rāga*).

Furthermore, although shamelessness (*āhrīkya*), lack of dread (*anapatrāpya*), restlessness (*auddhatya*), lethargy (*styāna*), distraction (*vikṣepa*), lack of faith (*āśraddhya*), and laziness (*kausīdya*) possess distinct natures of their own, they are of the nature of outflows (*niṣyanda*) from those aforementioned primary afflictions.
They are also called secondary afflictions (*upakleśa*), because they arise having the root afflictions as their cause.
Regarding the commentary’s mention of the "sixteen major secondary afflictions": among the twenty secondary afflictions, there are three grades—namely, minor, medium, and major.

The ten beginning with anger (*krodha*) are termed "minor secondary afflictions" (*parīttakleśabhūmika*) because they arise individually from their own kind and do not necessarily co-occur with others.

They may be either great or simultaneous. Because their activity and status are restricted, they are termed "small. Lack of shame (*āhrīkya*) and lack of dread (*anapatrāpya*) are called the "intermediate associates" (*madhya-anuvartin*), because they obtain concomitance with their own kind.
Anger (*krodha*) and the others are restricted solely to unwholesome states; thus, the latter eight only receive the name "intermediate.

As for the eight beginning with restlessness (*auddhatya*), they obtain concomitant arising with their own kind; since they are all pervasive within defiled states and obtain concomitant arising, [the restriction] cannot apply.
They are called "small" because they are common to all defilements; thus, they cannot be called "middling. Since these two meanings differ, the eight [mental factors] are called "great.

As for the current mention of "sixteen," this is because in both the form and formless realms there are restlessness (*auddhatya*), lethargy (*styāna*), lack of faith (*āśraddhya*), laziness (*kausīdya*), heedlessness (*pramāda*), loss of mindfulness (*muṣitasmṛti*), distraction (*vikṣepa*), and lack of correct knowledge (*asamprajanya*); thus, sixteen are established.
The commentary states: "The three realms together contain [fifteen]... called the outflow of ignorance (*avidyā-āsrava*). Each realm has five types of light;
when the three realms are discussed collectively, they constitute fifteen. According to the *Yogācārabhūmi-śāstra*, fascicle 89:

"All afflictions (*kleśa*) bound to the desire realm, with the exception of ignorance alone, are termed 'desires' (*kāma*). All afflictions bound to the two realms of form (*rūpa*) and formlessness (*arūpya*)..."

Excluding only ignorance (*avidyā*), these are called "tainted" (*sāsrava*). All lack of wisdom (*ajñāna*) existing within those three realms is subsumed as one and established as the "outflow of ignorance.
According to the Hīnayāna, forty-one factors constitute the essence of the "outflow of desire" (*kāma-āsrava*).

That is to say, there are thirty-one fundamental afflictions (*kleśa*) bound to the desire realm, and together with the ten envelopments (*paryavasthāna*), they form forty-one; when combined with the [other categories], they amount to fifty-two entities.
The essence of the outflows with taints (*āsrava*) refers to the fundamental afflictions (*kleśa*) of the two upper realms, which are termed twenty-six.

When divided by the five categories (*pañca-varga*) or the middle [categories], and excluding anger (*pratigha*) and delusion (*moha*) from each of the two realms respectively, they total fifty-two when combined. The five types of ignorance (*avidyā*) belonging to the three realms total fifteen, constituting the outflow of ignorance (*avidyā-āsrava*).
Question: Why are the two upper realms combined as the outflow with taints? Answer: Because they are identical in being of an indeterminate nature (*avyākṛta*).

Therefore: (1) because both operate within the internal door (*antarmukha*); (2) because both belong to the stage of meditative concentration (*samāhitabhūmi*). Due to these three meanings, the two realms are combined into one.

Regarding the commentary on the establishment and rejection of "separation" and "combination": the outflow of desire (*kāmāsrava*) is called "separation," while the outflow of existence (*bhavāsrava*) is called "combination.
Within these two outflows, ignorance (*avidyā*) is not included; this is termed "rejection" (*he*), as it is separately designated as an outflow. Thus it is said.
Regarding the commentary’s statement that it possesses the four modes of birth: these refer to the womb-born, egg-born, moisture-born, and transformation-born.

Regarding the commentary’s statement that it possesses one mode of birth and one type of affliction: "one mode of birth" refers exclusively to the nature of transformation-birth; "affliction" refers exclusively to the nature of obscured-unspecified (nivṛtāvyākṛta) states.

Regarding the statement that "associated and non-associated [ignorance] serve as the basis for the former two": there are two types of ignorance—first, associated (*saṃprayukta*), and second, non-associated (*āveṇika*).
That which coexists with craving and so forth is associated ignorance; that which does not coexist with craving and so forth is called independent (*svatantra*) ignorance.
Furthermore, non-associated ignorance is of two kinds: first, constant (*nitya*) non-associated ignorance, which exists only in the seventh [consciousness].
The second is the independent and unshared [ignorance], which refers to that which arises as a solitary mental factor within the sixth consciousness.
Regarding its being the basis for the former two: this outflow of ignorance serves as the locus of support for the former two outflows of desire and existence.
Regarding the commentary’s statement, “because it possesses eleven superior characteristics,” the *She* (攝) states: According to the *Pratītyasamutpāda-sūtra*, there are:

first, superiority of the object (*ālambana*), because it universally takes both the defiled and the pure as its objects; second, superiority of the aspect (*ākāra*), because it conceals the true and manifests the false;

third, superiority of the causal condition (*hetu-pratyaya*), because it is the root from which karma arises; fourth, superiority of the motivation (*samutthāna*), because it is equally able to initiate, to lead, to be led, and to produce.

1. Superiority of arising, because it is the dharma of dependent origination (*pratītyasamutpāda*). 2. Superiority of the fivefold transformation, because of the fourfold transformation of the latent tendencies (*anuśaya*), the envelopments (*paryavasthāna*), the associated [factors], and the non-common [factors].
3. Superiority of wrong practice, because of the practice of superimposition (*samāropa*) and denial (*apavāda*) regarding the truths (*satya*). 4. Superiority of characteristics (*lakṣaṇa*).
1. Superiority of subtle self-characteristic: because it functions pervasively throughout the aspect of pervasive anxiety (*sarvatraga-daurmanasya*). 2. Superiority of activity:

because it acts as the basis for the process of saṃsāra and acts as the obstacle to the state of peace (*śānti*). 3. Superiority of obstruction: because it obstructs the superior dharmas and the extensive dharmas. 4. Superiority of conformity:
because it continues to conform even up to the Peak of Existence (*bhavāgra*). 5. Superiority of antidote: [it consists of] the two kinds of sublime wisdom (*prajñā*).
Because it serves as an antidote, and because this ignorance possesses both associated and unique [defilements], as well as the eleven distinguished attributes and so forth,
it is established separately from the other afflictions as a distinct "outflow" (*āsrava*).

Regarding the statement in the commentary that "the afflictions of the lower realms mostly arise conditioned by desire," the *She* (攝) states: "To speak briefly, this refers to the 'Desire Realm' (*kāmadhātu*). Yet, there are three types of desire:
first, the desire for food and drink; second, the desire for sleep; and third, the desire for sexual intercourse. Because these are predominant, it receives the name 'Desire [Realm']."
The commentary states: "By virtue of the absence of either the manifest or the seeds, one attains true mastery. "Manifest" refers to the exhaustion of all outflows (*āsrava*);
"seeds" refers to the absence of further afflictions (*kleśa*). Because both of these are absent, it is called the attainment of true mastery.

Regarding the statement in the *Śāstra* that "having already abandoned the obstacles to concentration (samādhy-āvaraṇa), it is called 'liberation of mind' (*citta-vimukti*)," the *Viniścaya-saṃgrahaṇī* asks: What are these obstacles to concentration? It answers:
In principle, all defilements (*kleśa*) that are capable of obstructing concentration are truly called "obstacles.

However, according to the predominant [view], the "rebirth-experience" (*upapatti-bhava-vedanīya-karma*) of a different lineage is designated as the "predominant obstacle to concentration," because by experiencing inferior states, one does not advance upward. [The opponent] asks: Since concentration is thus mixed with obstacles, why is it called "mind"?
"Is it liberation? Answer: It is certainly a mental factor (*caitta*). It is named "liberation" because it follows its sovereign [the mind]; this is an explanation based on proximity (*upacāra*).

Alternatively, since concentration causes the mind to abide in a single object, concentration itself receives the name "mind. Furthermore, regarding those liberated through wisdom (*prajñā-vimukta*), since the hindrance of concentration does not apply to them, by what means do they enter the path of seeing (*darśana-mārga*)?
The *Vijñaptimātratāsiddhi* states: "By relying upon a superior basis (*āśraya*), they enter the path of seeing."
There are two interpretations of the answer. One says: one enters the untainted state by relying on the preparatory concentrations (*sāmantaka-samādhi*);

thus, the attainment of these preparatory concentrations does not necessarily belong to the hindrances. Another says: one also attains the four fundamental dhyānas, which likewise belong to the hindrances of concentration. Regarding the term "manifestation" (*saṃdarśana*):
it indicates that [the hindrance] can belong to the hindrances of concentration and so forth, but it does not belong to other hindrances of concentration, nor can it belong to them.

Regarding the phrase "because it is a hindrance to detachment": the very nature (*svabhāva*) of the afflictions (*kleśa*) is the hindrance; therefore, it is called a "hindrance of nature" (*prakṛti-āvaraṇa*).

This is a *karmadhāraya* (appositional) compound. Regarding the phrase "it distances that associated mind... [until] the liberation of the mind": "that" refers to those aforementioned factors such as ignorance, craving, and attachment. If...
The mind-king has not yet been freed from that ignorance and so forth, or from its associated [afflictions], and thus remains bound;
however, by being freed from ignorance and from the mind-king associated with craving, it attains liberation from bondage, and is therefore called "liberation of the mind" (citta-vimukti).

The Commentary states: "By being free from these two, one realizes the unconditioned (*asaṃskṛta*). This means that by being free from the two obstacles of nature (*prakṛti*) and meditative absorption (*samādhi*), one attains the unconditioned.

Furthermore, there are two types [of unconditioned attainment]. Although one has not yet attained the unconditioned of analytical cessation (*pratisaṃkhyā-nirodha*), one attains non-analytical cessation (*apratisaṃkhyā-nirodha*) by suppressing the obstacle to meditative absorption.

There is no logical error here. Since this meditative hindrance (*samādhi-āvaraṇa*) is subsumed under the cognitive hindrance (*jñeya-āvaraṇa*), it follows that attaining freedom from the meditative hindrance does not mean one has attained liberation.
[The text] states:
"The one who is distant from the seer... the one free from bondage, the one free from association—this is the essence of the King, and not bondage."
When [the mind] arises in association with or simultaneously with [afflictions], it subsequently becomes bound by the afflictions associated with it;

this is called "associated bondage" (*saṃprayoga-bandhana*), where "association" is itself the "bonding," according to the *karmadhāraya* (appositional) compound. As for "object-bound" (*ālambana-bandhana*), such as the objects of the five sense-fields, their essential nature is not itself bondage.
The essence of that cognizing mind is itself the bondage. When it binds its object, it is called "bondage of the object" (*ālambana-bandhana*).

This is an *ṣaṣṭhī-tatpuruṣa* (genitive determinative) compound. Thus, a verse in the *Abhidharmakośa-bhāṣya* says: "The various wonderful objects of the world are not true desire; true desire refers to the conceptual greed of humans.
Wonderful objects remain as they were in the world, but for the knower, desire has already been removed from among them. It further states:

The "associated" (saṃprayukta) refers to the seeing-part (*darśana-bhāga*); the "object-conditioned" (*ālambana*) refers to the image-part (*nimitta-bhāga*). Because these seeing and image parts infuse the seeds of afflictions, they are called "bonds.
The commentary states that those who are free from the two bonds of active outflows (*kleśa*) mean they are free from the two bonds of association and object-conditioning.

It is called "having no further afflictions. Question: Regarding the various outflows (*āsrava*), only their active manifestation (*samudācāra*) is mentioned. If one has no afflictions, it means there are no seeds (*bīja*).
How can it be said that one is free from them even while manifesting, yet not belonging to the seeds, by virtue of being far removed from both the seer and the seen?

It is called "free from afflictions. Answer: This refers exclusively to praising the Arhat; it does not speak of other persons. Therefore, there is none in the present, and necessarily none in the seeds.

Regarding the commentary’s statement, "Alternatively, the two views [of existence and non-existence] regarding the sprout," this does not use the second phrase to explain the third phrase. It is capable of...
The "seer" is the mind capable of grasping at a self; the "seen" is the characteristic of a self that is grasped.

If one is separated from the root of self-grasping, then the characteristic of a self that is grasped will no longer manifest within the consciousness of the present mind. This is like a mirror suspended in a high hall where an image appears within it:
the mirror is a metaphor for the seeing mind, and the image is a metaphor for the seen characteristic of a self. When there is a mirror, the image necessarily...
It appears therein; yet if the mirror is removed, the reflection will certainly not arise. Since the reflection does not arise in the absence of the mirror, by what cause could it have originated?
This is also the case here: if one is separated from the grasping mind that perceives a self, then the characteristics of the grasped self will likewise not appear.

Regarding the commentary’s preceding section from "the exhaustion of all outflows" to "contradiction," this addresses that contradiction. Furthermore, an external critic asks: "By means of the view of non-self and so forth, you explain the absence of afflictions;
how does this differ from the second phrase of the previous treatise on the exhaustion of outflows, which also explains the absence of afflictions?"

Therefore, this assembly states: while the previous mention of "the exhaustion of all outflows" refers to the general absence of afflictions (*kleśa*), the present statement regarding "the absence of afflictions" refers specifically to the absence of the view of self (*ātmadṛṣṭi*).
Since the view of self is the root from which all afflictions arise, it is explained here in terms of the absence of that view; thus, there is no contradiction.
Regarding the phrase "because the corresponding tasks have been accomplished," the *Śāstra* (Commentary) states:

"The various minds and mental factors that can realize or extinguish the Truth of Cessation (*nirodha-satya*) are termed 'corresponding' (*saṃprayukta*). The word 'like' (*yathā*) is a term of specification.

Because such corresponding tasks have already been accomplished, it is called 'accomplishing what is to be accomplished. Furthermore, it says: 'Like the corresponding [factors],' etc., is an illustration."
There are further explanations, but they are omitted here as they would be too prolix.
Regarding the passage from "This [text] has nine fetters" up to "established as fetters," the *Abhidharmasamuccaya-bhāṣya*, chapter six, states:

"In this context, it should be understood that the various fetters are explained by way of their characteristics (*lakṣaṇa*), their functions (*vṛtti*), and their stages (*avasthā*) to distinguish their differences. As for 'characteristics,' the fetter of craving (*anunaya-saṃyojana*) refers to the three..."

The fetter of attachment to the realms (*dhātu-rāga*). The fetter of ill-will (*pratigha-saṃyojana*) refers to the mental affliction of harming sentient beings and phenomena conducive to suffering; it is exclusively the anger (*vyāpāda*) of the desire realm.

The fetter of pride (*māna-saṃyojana*) refers to the seven types of pride, namely pride, excessive pride, and so forth. The fetter of ignorance (*avidyā-saṃyojana*) refers to the fifteen instances of ignorance in total across the three realms, which constitute the fetter of ignorance.
The fetter of views (*dṛṣṭi-saṃyojana*) refers to the view of a self-identity (*satkāya-dṛṣṭi*), false views (*mithyā-dṛṣṭi*), and [extreme views].

The fetter of views (*dṛṣṭi-saṃyojana*) refers to the view of grasping at views (*dṛṣṭi-parāmarśa*) and the view of grasping at precepts and observances (*śīla-vrata-parāmarśa*). The fetter of doubt (*vicikitsā-saṃyojana*) refers to hesitation regarding the Truths and uncertainty concerning the Triple Gem.
The fetter of envy (*īrṣyā-saṃyojana*) refers to being attached to gain and honor, being unable to endure the prosperity of others, and giving rise to mental malice.

The fetter of avarice (*mātsarya-saṃyojana*) refers to being attached to gain and honor, and being stingy with one's means of subsistence. These latter two types are both included among the secondary afflictions (*upakleśa*).

Regarding "function" (*vṛtti*): this refers to one who, possessing such [afflictions], does not grow weary of the triple world (*tridhātu*). Due to this, unwholesome states (*akuśala*) proceed in succession while wholesome states (*kuśala*) do not manifest;

by means of this, one is able to summon the suffering of future lives and becomes associated with that suffering. Regarding the "stage of verbal expression" (*pada-vāda*): this refers to the stage when the fruit of suffering arises in a subsequent life.
According to the *Yogācārabhūmi-śāstra*, fascicle 89, nine factors must be present for [the fruit] to be fully integrated.

Therefore, nine distinct fetters (*saṃyojana*) are established: first, based on the category of householders, the matter of the entanglement of craving for all objects, whether they be sentient beings or non-sentient things that are desirable;
second, based on this same category, the matter of the entanglement of aversion toward all objects, whether they be sentient beings or non-sentient things that are undesirable;
third, based on sentient beings, the matter of the entanglement of pride; and fourth, fifth, and sixth... [as follows].
Based on the teaching of false dharma, there are three types of perverse adherence regarding the matters that entangle those in the class of renunciants:
namely, based on hearing what is not the true dharma, based on improper and perverse reflection, and based on cultivation that is not encompassed by skillful means.
Such distinctions constitute three types: (7) the occurrence of the entanglement (*paryavasthāna*) of lack of resolute conviction (*anadhimukti*) regarding the well-spoken Dharma and Vinaya;

(8) the occurrence of poverty in wisdom (*prajñādāridrya*) based on the class of those who have gone forth (*pravrajita*); and (9) the occurrence of poverty in wealth (*dhanadāridrya*) based on the class of householders (*gṛhin*). Question:

Why, among the entanglements (*paryavasthāna*), are only the two—envy (*īrṣyā*) and avarice (*mātsarya*)—specifically established as "fetters" (*saṃyojana*)? Answer: According to the *Abhidharmakośa*, it is because envy and avarice alone...

They are of an unwholesome nature. Furthermore, this envy (*īrṣyā*) and avarice (*mātsarya*) arise solely through their own power; they do not follow others but arise by their own strength alone, and are thus called "independent" (*svatantra*).

Because they are superior in two respects, they are established separately as "fetters" (*saṃyojana*) among the "envelopments" (*paryavasthāna*). It is further said that they are so established due to seven reasons: first, because they manifest frequently;
second, because they are the causes of low status and poverty—envy being the cause of low status and avarice being the cause of poverty; third...

First, because they universally manifest secondary afflictions (*upakleśa*); that is, they universally manifest the secondary afflictions of arrogance (*mada*) and complacency (*pramada*). Second, because they disturb both the monastic and lay communities;

that is, the monastics are disturbed by envy (*īrṣyā*) and avarice (*mātsarya*) regarding the Dharma and its teachings, while the laity are disturbed by envy and avarice regarding wealth and material goods.
Third, because they may disturb the gods (*deva*) and asuras; that is, Śakra, Lord of the Devas, possesses the flavor of ambrosia (*amṛta-rasa*), whereas the asuras— [text continues].

The *asuras* possess the beauty of women; the gods are stingy regarding flavors and jealous of their beauty, while the *asuras* are stingy regarding their own beauty and jealous of the flavors [of the gods].

Consequently, they give rise to strife and contention. Sixth, it is because they disturb and confuse humans and those in the superior realms. Seventh, it is because they afflict others and themselves. "Group" (*bhu*) means a multitude.
This means that stinginess afflicts one's own group, while envy afflicts the friends of others; it is for these seven reasons stated above that it is so called.
Furthermore, among the nine fetters (*saṃyojana*), five are dull afflictions (*mṛdu-kleśa*) and two are sharp afflictions (*tīkṣṇa-kleśa*).
The Commentary states that from the phrase "by accomplishing the aforementioned points" up to "the state of mastery," this mind attains mastery because it possesses all the aforementioned points;

thus, one attains the state of mastery over the mind. The Sub-commentary (*Śāstra*) says: Question: Since the name "mastery of mind" is derived from these various points, why is it explained as a single term?

Answer: The Master of the Commentary speaks of them collectively; by possessing the aforementioned points, one reaches mastery of mind, which is distinct from the other individual points. He takes [this as the primary meaning].
He comes to explain [the term].

Regarding the commentary’s reference to the *Śāstra*’s three types of single explanations and so forth: Question: Now, regarding the "superior-superior" (*uttarottara*) progression, it is named by explaining the superior through the inferior.
Why is it called "superior-superior arising" when there are three single [explanations] and two non-explanations? Answer: As for what is called "superior-superior arising," it proceeds from...
Generally speaking, those of that category may also receive that name. Some people establish four permutations (catuṣkoṭi) for both "arising from below" and "arising from above.
Regarding the four permutations of arising from above and below: first, following the pattern of what is below but not above, as in the second phrase explaining the first phrase;
second, following the pattern of what is above but not below, as in the second phrase explaining the third phrase; and third, likewise...
Regarding "above" and "below": as in the case of attaining true mastery (*vaśitā*) and so forth, the four [categories] that are neither below nor above can be understood accordingly.

Furthermore, regarding "immediate succession" (*anantara*) and "separation" (*vyavahita*), there are four permutations (*catuṣkoṭi*): 1. Immediate succession and not separation: as explained in the second phrase for the first phrase.
2. Separation and not immediate succession: as explained in the fourth phrase for the second phrase, and so on. 3. The combined category: as explained in the fifth and sixth phrases for the seventh.

The sixth is the "adjacent" (*sāmantaka*); the fifth is the "separated. Furthermore, as in the ninth and tenth [sections] which explain the eighth phrase and so forth, the four "neither" (*ubhayābhāva*) cases can be understood.
Moreover, by combining the single and the multiple, four phrases are formed: first, the single that is not multiple, such as the explanation of the first phrase by the second phrase;
second, the multiple that is not single, such as the explanation of the seventh by the fifth and sixth; third, the combined phrase.

As with the fourth phrase, it is explained by means of the second and third; furthermore, the fourth phrase explains the second phrase and so forth, such that the four phrases are mutually non-existent. This may be understood.
The Commentary states: "Now, relying on this scriptural passage" refers to the following explanation of the text.

The phrase "Therefore, upon entering the tenth stage, one obtains the name of Arhat" explains the meaning of the exhaustion of outflows (*āsravakṣaya*) as it manifests, and clarifies the reason for obtaining the title of Arhat.
This means that for a Bodhisattva of sudden enlightenment, the seeds of innate afflictions (*sahaja-kleśa*) still remain throughout the ten stages.

He is named an Arhat because he has realized that all outflows (*āsrava*) within him have been exhausted; these are merely those currently manifesting. Furthermore, this refers specifically to one aspect and does not pertain to the seeds.

Regarding the commentary’s statement, “either the outflows are entirely exhausted or specific attachments are also lost”: "entirely exhausted" refers to the two types of cultivation—the cultivation of the associated [mind] and the cultivation of the object—which constitute the total exhaustion of outflows. That is to say:

The second phrase. "Distinct" refers to the grasping of the view of self (*ātmadṛṣṭi*). Because of the view of self, the various outflows (*āsrava*) arise; now, regarding afflictions, the intention here is to take up the view of self.
Since the various outflows are exhausted, the view of self perishes accordingly; thus, being far removed from these two views is called "being without affliction.
The two views refer to the characteristics of the self as both the grasper and the grasped. *She* (the commentary) says: this constitutes the meaning of the phrase itself and its underlying reason.

This refutes external objections. The previous statement regarding the "exhaustion of all outflows" (*āsravakṣaya*) was based on afflictions in their totality; in that regard, there is nothing further to say.

However, with respect to the specific [affliction] of self-grasping (*ātma-grāha*), although both [the general and the specific] manifest simultaneously, there is a distinction between the general and the specific. Therefore, the seeds of these two parts [of self-grasping] remain. This follows the former interpretation: that while there are no longer [general] afflictions, [specific ones may still persist].
This is the second explanation.

Regarding the commentary’s passage from “By this, [one cycles through] birth and death” to “the afflictions of the nine fetters”: the continuous flow of birth and death is called a heavy burden (*bhāra*).

Because one belongs to birth and death, it is called “discarding the heavy burden. Because one discards the heavy burden, one attains one’s own benefit (*ātman-hita*). This corresponds to the phrase “self-” in the verse.
[Commentary: This is not an interpretation based on the meaning of "casting off the heavy burden" found in that treatise, but rather an interpretation of "attaining one's own benefit.

Regarding the phrase in the sub-commentary (*śū*), "From the exhaustion of outflows above... to mastery": because all outflows (*āsrava*) have been exhausted, one reaches the bonds of existence within the realms.

These four phrases indicate that the afflictions (*kleśa*) of both the path of seeing (*darśanamārga*) and the path of cultivation (*bhāvanāmārga*) are entirely exhausted. Because one is detached from these afflictions, the mind becomes [liberated].

Regarding "obstructions to the nature and to matters": the obstruction to matters is precisely the obstruction to meditative concentration (*samādhi*). Because of the obstruction to concentration, and because concentration is the basis, one is able to give rise to supernormal powers (*abhijñā*);
by attaining mastery over these matters of supernormal power, it is called being "free from obstructions to matters."

Regarding the commentary’s statement, "Third, entering a village... or being disturbed," the *Shè* (Summary) says: For example, Udraka Rāmaputra, although he had attained the meditative absorption of neither-perception-nor-non-perception (*naivasaṃjñānāsaṃjñāyatana*), was not yet masterful in it.
Later, when he entered a royal palace, he was disturbed by the objects of desire; his prior possession of various supernormal powers (*abhijñā*) is precisely what is meant here.

Regarding the statement in the *Śāstra* that "one should exclusively lead [them] toward further cultivation," the *Shè* (Commentary) says: Question: Since they are designated as "those beyond training" (*aśaikṣa*), how can there be further cultivation?

Answer: Because those at the ultimate stage of the Two Vehicles aspire toward Great Bodhi. Objection: If this were so, those of fixed nature (*niyata-gotra*) would not engage in further cultivation. Answer:

They also delight in benefiting others, refining their faculties (*indriya-pariśodhana*), and eliminating obstacles; since these are collectively termed "further cultivation," there is no logical flaw.
Commentary 9: One should cite emptiness (*śūnyatā*) in relation to the practitioner. These—the ninth, tenth, and eleventh—are the three gates of liberation (*vimokṣamukha*).
They consist of contemplating the sixteen aspects (*ākāra*) underlying the Four Noble Truths. The meaning of these sixteen aspects will be clarified below.

Regarding the statement, "Because one does not give rise to attachment to the dhyānas of the three realms," the *Shu* (Commentary) says: Question: Dhyāna belongs only to the realm of form (*rūpadhātu*). What are its two types? Answer:
The formless realm (*ārūpyadhātu*) may also be designated as dhyāna. "Dhyāna" is translated here as *śamatha-vipaśyanā* (calm abiding and insight).
Because it can produce all meritorious qualities (*guṇa*), it is also meaningfully called a "grove of the accumulation of merit. Thus, the *Mahāprajñāpāramitā-śāstra*, fascicle 18, states:

Regarding "dhyāna" (meditative concentration): it refers to the four dhyānas, the four formless attainments (*ārūpya-samāpatti*), and other such meditative absorptions (*samādhi*). If this were not the case, the *dhyāna-pāramitā* would not fully encompass all forms of concentration.

Question: Why do the sūtras and śāstras not define those [formless attainments] as "dhyāna"? Answer: Because the form realm (*rūpa-dhātu*) possesses the full constituent factors (*aṅga*), whereas the formless realm does not;
thus, their names are distinguished. In actual principle, however, they are both equally present.

Regarding the commentary’s statement, “One should know [them] as they truly are... because of their merits”: for instance, among the class of ordinary beings (*pṛthagjana*), each is born separately according to their respective karma, and the various realms of existence are distinct;

thus, each is an ordinary being. Once one has entered the Path of Seeing (*darśanamārga*), all share the same aspiration toward the Path, observe the same principle, and possess the same Buddha-Dharma;
this is called being a "co-arisen" (*sahaja*). Now, within this state of being co-arisen, one attains the ultimate.
It is the ultimate fruit; therefore, it is called *pāramitā*. This means that within the Lesser Vehicle (*hīnayāna*), one has reached the other shore.

Having attained this fruit, one extensively delivers sentient beings, causing them to likewise attain the merits one has acquired for oneself. The *Shè* (攝) states: "According to the intent of the *Shù* (疏), it says:"
To transform all sentient beings so that they share in the benefits obtained by an Arhat oneself is called "being born together" (*sahaja*).

This interpretation is correct. Regarding the commentary from "the successive stages of cultivation" up to "the distinct meaning": this is a detailed differentiation. As for the eighth stage, "cultivation without ceasing," and the twelfth, "not being attached to dhyāna," the intent is as follows:
when first advancing in the practice of various deeds, one does not cling to dhyāna; rather, one abandons the inferior and proceeds toward the superior.

Therefore, it subsequently belongs to the various fetters (*saṃyojana*). Regarding the statement in the commentary, "In meditative concentrations and the like, one does not become attached through relishing;
conditioned phenomena (*saṃskṛta*) can be described [up to] because they are different," this means that True Suchness (*tathatā*), based on its nature and characteristics, transcends language;

because it lies beyond the path of words, it is called "inexpressible. This does not mean that conditioned phenomena are expressible such that they could fully capture their own specific characteristics (*svalakṣaṇa*) through verbal expression. Even that falls short.
Therefore, based on their common characteristics (*sāmānya-lakṣaṇa*), it is provisionally said that they can be described.

Regarding the phrase "attaining the merit of inclusion" (*saṃgraha-pratilambha-guṇa*) in the Commentary (*Śū*), the *Śū* states: Question: What is meant by "attainment"? Answer: The intention of the *Śū* is as follows: [The text continues with the answer].
Because it accomplishes two phrases, one is thereby able to attain all meritorious virtues; therefore, it is called "attainment.

Regarding the commentary’s fifth point, "gathering the supreme virtues that ought to be performed," the sub-commentary (*śū*) says: Question: If one is still practicing offerings, why is it called "having already performed what was to be done"?
Answer: Because one's own virtues are fulfilled, it is called "having already performed what was to be done. Furthermore, in order to repay the Buddha's kindness...

Regarding the practice of making offerings, the commentary on the latter phrase states that those who transcend the lower and upper realms: the desire realm is called "lower," while the form and formless realms are called "upper. Why is this so?
The answer is: because meditative concentration (*samādhi*) and distraction (*vikṣepa*) differ, they are divided into lower and upper.
Regarding the commentary’s eighth section on "comprehending the aforementioned virtues": Question: Why is this phrase [included]?
In the fourteenth section of the preceding "Gate of Arising," it was stated that right knowledge and liberation (*samyag-jñāna-vimukti*) are unconditioned (*asaṃskṛta*).

In the thirteenth section of the second "Gate of General and Particular Characteristics," it was stated that right knowledge and liberation are precisely what are called the supernormal powers (*abhijñā*). Now, within these aforementioned virtues, they are treated as unconditioned.

Regarding the fruit: because it is the most supreme among all virtues, there is this distinction. In the response concerning the "Gate of Arising as Most Supreme," it is described as unconditioned (*asaṃskṛta*) with respect to that which is realized;
however, with respect to the realizing agent, correct wisdom (*samyag-jñāna*) is indeed conditioned (*saṃskṛta*).

In the second section, the "Gate of General and Specific Conceptions," with respect to that correct wisdom, it is able to give rise to supernormal powers (*abhijñā*) in order to transform sentient beings. Question: Why?
Therefore, in both places, it is said that they are "liberated. Answer: The former is based on the fact that [defilements] have perished, which is termed "liberation";

this [latter] is based on the objective reality that supernatural powers (*abhijñā*) are not provisional, which is termed "liberation. Thus, the first two types are both called "liberation. Now, regarding the term "unconditioned" (*asaṃskṛta*) in the third section:
this refers to the fact that through correct wisdom (*samyagjñāna*), one realizes the unconditioned fruit; it is a praise of these virtues of the unconditioned fruit.
Among these, it is the most supreme.

Regarding the commentary’s statement, "The ninth [section] on the merit of gathering sentient beings": a question arises as to whether the mastery of mind (*citta-vaśitā*) clarified here within the state of *yathābhūta-citta-vaśitā* is the same as the stage of mastery of mind clarified in the previous two gates.
Now, in this third gate, from the perspective of external transformation (*parārtha*), it is termed "self-... [the text here appears to be truncated].
The preceding section explained [the path] in terms of self-benefit; this third section explains it in terms of both self-benefit and the benefit of others.
Regarding the commentary on the *Vijñaptimātratāsiddhi* (from "until" to "because they arise"): the following belongs to the section on exclusion (*viveka*). First, the text is cited;
subsequently, from the point where the preceding section opens its thematic gate, the explanation is applied. This is the first [part].
The Commentary on the Section on the Comprehension of Matters (up to the phrase "only those liberated both ways"):

This means that while the three types of arhats described in the *Vijñaptimātratāsiddhi* are generally applicable to all arhats who are liberated through both wisdom and meditative concentration, this present section on the comprehension of matters speaks specifically of ten kinds of meritorious qualities;
thus, it refers exclusively to arhats liberated both ways. Because this category is so restrictive, it does not include the other three types. [This concludes] the first two sections.
[The term] "middle" applies in meaning to all arhats; therefore, it is specifically assigned [to this category]. Question: In the first two gates, the ten virtues were not mentioned.
Since these apply to all arhats, both of those [gates] should encompass all three [categories]. Why, then, does the first gate encompass two and the second encompasses one? Answer:
They are assigned in this way because they are manifested according to their specific meanings. Since, in the first gate, all outflows (*āsrava*) have already been exhausted...
To exhaust all fetters of existence (*bhava-saṃyojana*) is precisely what it means to "eternally destroy the thief," in the sense that there is no further segmentation [of rebirth].
This is because in the second section, it is stated that one should receive food, drink, bedding, and so forth; therefore, this correspondence is made based on these similar characteristics.

The Commentary further explains the "Gate of Arising from the Highest" (up to the point of) "segmented [existence]": this is the gate of arising for birth. Because their outflows (*āsrava*) have been exhausted, they are called Arhats and so forth.

Since these are mostly outflow-afflictions (*kleśa*), they are assigned to the "affliction-thieves" who are to be slain. In the *Tongbie xiangmen lun* (Treatise on the General and Specific Characteristics), fifteen kinds of meanings regarding "one worthy of" (*arhat*) are clarified;
therein it says that because they "are worthy of receiving food and drink," they are assigned to being "capable of receiving sublime offerings" and thus "gathering [them]."
In the *Vastusamgrahaṇī*, because it elucidates the ten types of conditioned and unconditioned qualities, it is assigned to birth without interruption (*apratīsaṃdhi-jāti*).
This assignment is made according to the majority of cases; it does not mean that this characteristic exists in its entirety [in all instances].
Regarding the phrase "The matching of the meaning of the commentary’s thesis is irrational and not definitive," this means that such a matching is merely the method of the school's followers;
it does not mean that the author of the treatise, nor the ultimate truth, has determined it to be so. This is merely a matter of human sentiment being taken as a standard for application.
